explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma during pregnancy is presence of a quickly developing vascular mass on the skin or mucous membranes. The clinical diagnosis requires excisional biopsy for confirmation.1 Because of the hemorrhagic nature of pyogenic granulomas, the biopsy should be performed as an excisional biopsy by an oral surgeon.1-3 Although intralesional steroids have been used in some recurrent cases, oral steroids are not effective. Watchful waiting is an option when the lesion is very small, not bleeding, not enlarging, and does not interfere with eating; however, because this patient’s lesion was large and bleeding and also making it difficult for her to eat, excision was warranted.1-3Pyogenic granuloma, also called lobular capillary hemangioma (or, during pregnancy, “pregnancy tumor” or granuloma gravidarum), is a benign, fast-growing, vascular tumor with friable surfaces that can occur on the skin or mucous membranes. Roughly 2% to 5% of pregnant women develop intraoral pyogenic granuloma within the first 5 months of pregnancy.3,4 Theories for pathogenesis during pregnancy include promotion of angiogenesis, hormonal influence, and trauma (from aggressive oral care, which accounts for 30% of cases).1,2,5 In nonpregnant patients, drug-induced cases from antineoplastic, monoclonal antibody, retinoid, and immunosuppressive agents have been reported.2,3The lesion often starts as a small red papule that undergoes rapid growth initially and then stabilizes. Pyogenic granulomas in pregnancy sometimes regress or resolve after childbirth.6 In cases unrelated to pregnancy, spontaneous resolution is rare. Common clinical presentations can range from asymptomatic to severe, with bleeding, pain, and discomfort while eating. The differential diagnosis commonly includes hemangioma, peripheral giant cell granuloma (an exophytic lesion seen in the gingiva that would have more of a bluish hue), amelanotic melanoma (a melanoma that lacks normal pigment), squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, common wart, and Kaposi sarcoma (which most commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients).2,7Treatment of choice for most patients is surgical excision that extends down to the periosteum, except in cases in which excision would cause significant deformity. After excision, there is potential for recurrence in up to 16% of patients. Laser therapy, electrocautery, cryotherapy, and sclerotherapy are newer modalities that show promise and may be used to decrease scarring and deformity. Another option is watchful waiting, especially in pregnancy if the lesion is small, not bleeding, and not bothersome to the patient. Intralesional steroids are used for recurrent pyogenic granulomas. Topical therapy with imiquimod, phenol, or topical β-blockers has also been used.1-4,7 After treatment of an oral pyogenic granuloma, careful oral hygiene with soft toothbrushes and removal of dental plaque to prevent further irritation near the gum line are important to prevent recurrence of the lesion.2The patient underwent excision of the mass at 27 weeks’ gestation, and the diagnosis of pyogenic granuloma was confirmed. The area healed well, and there were no recurrences during the remainder of the pregnancy. She went on to deliver a healthy infant at 39 weeks’ gestation.

explanation: Ring melanoma is a rare form of uveal melanoma that grows in a circumferential pattern, involving 6 or more clock hours of the ciliary body1 and/or anterior chamber angle.2 The differential diagnosis of a pigmented iridociliary lesion also includes nevus, melanocytoma, iris pigment epithelium adenoma, or cyst, but these are typically localized and circumscribed. Ring melanoma is often difficult to diagnose owing to its ability to hide beneath the scleral overhang2 or mimic other disease entities. It has been misdiagnosed as pigmentary glaucoma, iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, traumatic angle recession, iridocyclitis, and ciliary body detachment.1,3Most patients with ring melanoma are asymptomatic; however, lenticular astigmatism, cataract, or accommodative dysfunction from ciliary body involvement may cause blurred vision.1 The tumor may also present with symptoms of increased intraocular pressure3 because of invasion of the angle or melanomalytic glaucoma with impedance of aqueous outflow by pigment-laden macrophages within the trabecular meshwork.4Ring melanoma is most commonly brown and multilobulated but can also be amelanotic5 and in dome, mushroom, or flat configurations.1 Examination may also reveal ocular hypertension, sentinel vessels, iris neovascularization, sectoral cataract, and serous retinal or choroidal detachment.1-3,6 Ultrasound biomicroscopy aids in the determination of tumor thickness and circumferential extension, while gonioscopy is essential to determine involvement of angle structures.3Fine-needle aspiration biopsy may be performed, but ring melanoma is usually established clinically.7 Transvitreal biopsy cannot be easily performed on lesions anterior to the equator. Metastatic screening should be performed to exclude distal metastases prior to any disfiguring eye surgery. Treatment is largely limited to enucleation,1 as ring melanomas are typically too large to resect by iridocyclectomy, and there is a significant risk of local recurrence with radiotherapy owing to the lack of appropriately designed plaques and microscopic spread within the angle.2,8 Radiotherapy may result in glaucoma refractory to medical therapy.4,9Ring melanoma most frequently spreads hematogenously to the liver1 and is associated with a poorer prognosis than other forms of uveal melanoma. The estimated 5-year incidence of metastasis for ciliary body ring melanoma is 52%,1 and 25% of anterior chamber angle ring melanomas developed metastases after a median of 3.9 years.2The patient elected to undergo enucleation (Figure 2). Given the natural history of ring melanoma, this patient is observed with a high-risk screening protocol, including semiannual computed tomography scans of the abdomen and an annual chest radiograph. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits did not show evidence of orbital extension. The patient underwent an incisional biopsy, which revealed extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated tissues on histopathology and immunohistochemistry. A staging computed tomography scan showed no adenopathy elsewhere, and radiation therapy of the orbit was therefore recommended. Subconjunctival mass in the fornix prior to biopsy.Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma is the most frequent type of non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma occurring in the conjunctiva. It typically presents in patients 70 years and older as a slow-growing salmon patch lesion in the fornix, with a slight predominance in women. Its pathogenesis is thought to involve chronic inflammation from antigenic stimulation, infection, or autoimmune processes.1Terrien marginal degeneration is a slowly progressive, commonly bilateral, painless degenerative ectasia of the peripheral cornea, occurring most often in men older than 40 years.2 It is most frequently seen in the superior cornea, where stromal thinning or furrowing with lipid deposition at the leading anterior edge is seen. Vision loss due to irregular against-the-rule astigmatism and, in rare cases, perforations can occur. Treatment options generally entail correction of the astigmatism with a rigid gas permeable contact lens, lamellar keratoplasty, or corneal patch graft if perforation is imminent. While the exact mechanism behind the condition is unknown, inflammation is generally not a prominent feature,3 unlike with Mooren ulcer, although some studies suggest an inflammatory variant.4,5 This case was less typical for Terrien degeneration in that it was completely unilateral and that it eventually developed pronounced inflammation and neovascularization.In cases of lipid keratopathy from corneal neovascularization without another known cause, there have been reports of regression of both vessels and lipids after injections of subconjunctival anti–vascular endothelial growth factor  agents, such as bevacizumab.6 In this patient, this was not the treatment of choice, as the patient had another, more pressing diagnosis that was likely contributing to the corneal findings.In this patient, it is possible that indolent, chronic inflammation from the cornea served as antigenic stimulation for the formation of extranodal marginal zone lymphoma in the adjacent conjunctiva. question: A man in his 40s presented with gradual hair loss of the eyelashes, eyebrows, beard, and scalp for 4 years, swelling and painful hand joints for 13 months, and multiple asymptomatic nodules on the upper arms for 40 days. The patient exhibited no associated fever, analgesia or hypesthesia. He reported no previous infections or family or personal medical history of autoimmune diseases or psoriasis. He was previously treated for rheumatoid arthritis, but various arthritis treatments showed no improvements over 1 year. A physical examination showed diffuse infiltration of the face with loss of skin creases and diminished facial hair; all joints of both hands were swollen (Figure, A); multiple asymptomatic nodules without ulceration were present on his upper arms (Figure, B); decreased sensation to pain, temperature and/or touch and neuropathic changes were not found. Laboratory test results showed a slightly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h) and significantly elevated rheumatoid factor (70.1 IU/mL). Additional immunology indicators, including C-reactive protein, anticyclic citrullinated peptide, antinuclear antibodies, and globulin levels were normal. X-ray and joint ultrasound results suggested osteoarthritis, synovitis, flexor tendon tenosynovitis, and bone erosions. Ultrasound results also indicated enlarged axillary, cervical, and inguinal lymph nodes and an enlarged spleen. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed uveitis.A, Joints of both hands were swollen. B, Multiple asymptomatic nodules on the upper arms. C, Skin biopsy from the patient’s upper arm nodule demonstrating diffuse infiltrate of foamy histiocytes in the dermis (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×100). D, Numerous acid-fast bacilli (acid-fast stain, original magnification ×400). What Is Your Diagnosis?
opc: Arthritis associated with other connective tissue diseases
explanation: The primary clinical features include the presence of swollen and painful hand joints, asymptomatic subcutaneous nodules, and gradual hair loss. The skin biopsy showed diffuse infiltrate of foamy histiocytes in the dermis with numerous acid-fast bacilli (Figure, C and D). These characteristics exclude other diagnoses such as rheumatic diseases, arthritis associated with other autoimmune diseases, and lupus. The clinical manifestations and histopathologic findings are consistent with the features of lepromatous leprosy with a type 2 leprosy reaction (T2R). The patient was treated effectively with multidrug therapy (rifampin, clofazimine, and dapsone) and thalidomide in the Leprosy Treatment Center in Shandong Province, China. Skin lesions substantially improved after 2 months of therapy, and the patient is currently receiving maintenance therapy with close follow-up.Leprosy is a chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae that primarily attacks the skin and peripheral nerves. The clinical presentation depends on the genetically determined cellular immunity of the patient. Accordingly, the disease is often categorized as multibacillary or paucibacillary (lepromatous or tuberculoid).1 In most patients, early leprosy presents with macular, hypopigmented lesions, and impaired sensory, motor, and autonomic functions of peripheral nerves.2 The pathogen transmission route is not well understood, and patients with susceptibility genes are prone to the infection.3Leprosy reactions are acute inflammatory episodes that may occur multiple times during the course of the disease or after treatment, manifesting as type 1 reaction (T1R) or T2R. A T1R (or reversal reactions) is clinically characterized by acutely inflamed preexisting skin lesions, the appearance of new lesions, edema of extremities, and/or neuritis.4 Type 1 reactions are delayed hypersensitivity reactions that usually present with edema, an increased number of lymphocytes in the dermis, and loss of normal granuloma organization in the histology.5 A T2R (erythema nodosum leprosum) typically presents as tender or painful subcutaneous nodules on the face or extensor surfaces of the limbs with associated fever and arthralgia in patients with a high bacilli load.6 Type 2 reactions are considered a form of small vessel vasculitis (cutaneous and systemic) owing to immune complex deposition; thus, vasculitis indicators might be increased.7 Therefore, patients with leprosy who have a T2R may often be misdiagnosed with rheumatic diseases, as in this case.A previous study8 confirmed T-cell unresponsiveness to Mycobacterium leprae owing to an increase in inhibitory regulator T (Treg) cells in stable nonreactive lepromatous leprosy patients. It shows that patients with leprosy reactions may have an imbalance in T helper 17 (Th17) cells and Treg populations.8 The reduced Treg suppressor activity is associated with higher Th17 cell activity owing to the combined effects of reduced transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) and increased interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-21 cytokines, contributing to lesional inflammation. question: A woman in her 20s presented to our department for treatment of multiple facial papules. The lesions were present since childhood, progressively increasing in number. They involved primarily her face, and, less so, her extremities and trunk. There was no medical history of spontaneous regression. She had a young brother, who had the same papular lesions that had followed the same natural history, displaying a similar bodily distribution although fewer in number. Previous studies and imaging of the 2 siblings had failed to reveal any systemic findings.Physical examination revealed multiple smooth skin-colored and erythematous papules of various size, some with telangiectasia, with a medial but asymmetrical distribution on the face (Figure, A). Identical, less numerous lesions were also present on her hands and back. Three biopsy samples were taken and showed similar findings (Figure, B-D). A, Multiple skin-colored to erythematous asymptomatic facial papules in a woman in her 20s. The papules were present in childhood and were increasing in number. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×20). C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×40). D, Alcian blue stain (original magnification ×10). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: The biopsies showed dilated vessels, mucin deposits, in addition to a prominent histiocytic proliferation made of spindle or globular cells, which were CD68 positive, CD1a negative and S100 negative. There were neither abnormal follicular structures as may be seen in trichofolliculoma, nor perifollicular fibrosis. The dermis was much more cellular, with more mucin than what is observed in angiofibromas. Altogether, the familial history, clinical presentation, evolution and histopathology were suggestive of hereditary progressive mucinous histiocytosis (HPMH). Indeed, specimens examined under transmission electron microscopy revealed histiocytes with a cytoplasm rich in characteristic vacuoles. They formed zebra bodies containing stacked transverse lamellae, or, myelin bodies (vacuoles with concentric rings of myelin). No Birbeck granules were noted. The biopsy specimens from the younger brother showed similar histopathologic and electron microscopic features. We treated our patient with ablative CO2 laser (Sharplan, Lumenis industries, 10 watts) with good improvement. The results were maintained at 2 years of follow-up.Hereditary progressive mucinous histiocytosis is considered to be a type of a nonlangerhans cell histiocytosis.1 However, because of its rarity, it has not always been incorporated in classification models. To the best of our knowledge, 22 cases have been described in the literature worldwide. Of these, 17 were familial cases, presumed to present an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. The remaining 5 were sporadic cases.Hereditary progressive mucinous histiocytosis seems to present with 2 distinct phases in patients with the inherited variant. The first phase is seen in infancy and is characterized by dermal nodules that can be seen on the scalp, trunk, and extremities. These lesions regress spontaneously.2,3 It is unclear whether the infantile stage is present in all patients. The second phase starts at a later stage, in childhood and up to early adulthood. Papules appear and keep progressing throughout life with no spontaneous resolution.2 They are smooth, skin-colored or erythematous to red brown, ranging from 1 to 10 mm in size. The lesions are generally asymptomatic, although mild pruritus has been occasionally described. Most common locations include face, scalp, hands, forearm and thighs. There is no associated mucosal, visceral, or systemic involvement and the course is benign. As opposed to other diseases on the differential of HPMH, the lack of systemic involvement makes the recognition of this entity particularly important. It allows to reassure patients on their prognosis and avoid unnecessary exams. Alternatively, patients with sporadic HPMH only develop the second phase lesions at a later age, from 30 to 60 years.3-6Reported histological findings are similar, ie, well-circumscribed aggregates of epithelioid and spindled histiocytes in the upper and mid dermis, with mucinous stroma, and dilated vessels.5 In addition, some reports found an increased number of mast cells. Although iron deposits in the dermis have been described, they are not consistently found in all patients.6 The lack of very specific clinical and histological findings makes the diagnosis difficult and often delayed, as was the case in our patient. Clinicopathological differential diagnosis includes dermatofibromas, other nonlangerhans cell histiocytoses, papular mucinosis, and adnexal tumors. Immunohistochemical staining shows a disparity for CD68 with some cases staining positive4,5,7 while others were negative.8-10 The staining is consistently negative for Langerhans cell markers CD1a and S100. The association of unusual histiocytic proliferation with mucin deposits is suggestive of the disease. Findings under electron microscopy are pathognomonic and reveal abundant vacuoles, myelin bodies, and zebra bodies in the cytoplasm of lesional histiocytes.2,8The progressive nature of HPMH differentiates it from nonlangerhans cell histiocytoses that present with lesions that regress spontaneously after a few years, such as multicentric reticulohistiocytosis or generalized eruptive histiocytoma. On the other hand, although nodular histiocytosis also follows a nonremitting course, it tends to have a more generalized distribution, bigger lesions with a central depression reaching up to 5 cm and associated systemic findings.5Treatment has been unrewarding. Topical steroids, cryotherapy, imiquimod, and pulsed dye laser have been tried with unsatisfactory results.2 Thalidomide (100mg/d), used in a woman in her 30s, resulted in a decrease in the size of the lesions while no new papules developed for the treatment duration.4 The best treatment modalities so far seem to be surgical removal or destruction of lesions.

explanation: The mixing study is a relatively simple procedure performed in the hemostasis laboratory by mixing the patient’s plasma with normal pooled plasma in a 1:1 ratio. Clotting tests will result in normal values when at least 50% of the activity of the involved coagulation factors is present.1 If the underlying problem is a factor production deficiency, mixing the patient’s plasma 1:1 with normal pooled plasma that contains 100% of the normal factor level will result in a level that is greater than or equal to 50% in the mixture. In this scenario, the prothrombin time or partial thromboplastin time will be normal, indicating a factor production deficiency. Failure to correct the clotting time in the mixing study indicates presence of an inhibitor. Some inhibitors take time to inhibit clotting factors in the normal pooled plasma. When this occurs, the 1:1 mix will have a normal coagulation when tested immediately but will yield an abnormal test result when incubated for 1 to 2 hours at 37°C. The Medicare midpoint reimbursement is $7.26 for a prothrombin time mixing study and $11.05 for a partial thromboplastin time mixing study.2 Despite some limitations, the mixing study helps guide further testing by determining whether coagulation factor testing or inhibitor testing should be performed next.The isolated prolonged partial thromboplastin time led to a differential diagnosis of inadequate levels of factors VIII (antihemophilic factor [AHF]), IX (plasma thromboplastin component [PTC]), or XI (plasma thromboplastin antecedent [PTA]) in the intrinsic pathway. Antibodies to factor VIII are the most common type of acquired hemophilia. Risk factors include older age, pregnancy or the postpartum state, rheumatologic disorders, malignancy, and drug reactions. However, no underlying disorder was present in 46% of cases based on a population-based study.3 The mainstay of treatment is control of bleeding and elimination of the inhibitor. Prednisone and the addition of cyclophosphamide, along with other immunosuppressants, have been studied, but no therapy is clearly superior.4Occasionally, mixing studies are not definitive, especially when a partial thromboplastin time is mildly prolonged and corrects with mixing. The patient simultaneously began treatment with a combination of prednisone, 1 mg/kg per day, and cyclophosphamide for immunosuppression to eradicate the inhibitor. Physical examination revealed a body mass index of 20 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared), normal vital signs, and darkening of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. opa: Evaluate for congenital adrenal hyperplasia with serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
opb: Evaluate for primary adrenal insufficiency with a 250-μg corticotropin stimulation test.
opc: Evaluate for a pituitary adenoma with magnetic resonance imaging.

answer: Evaluate for primary adrenal insufficiency with a 250-μg corticotropin stimulation test.
explanation: Cortisol is a steroid hormone secreted by the adrenal glands in response to stimulation by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH or corticotropin). In an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, ACTH and plasma cortisol levels follow a diurnal pattern and are at their highest in the morning and lowest in the evening. This circadian rhythm is disrupted in various conditions including Cushing syndrome (inappropriate hypersecretion of cortisol) and adrenal insufficiency (inappropriate hyposecretion of cortisol).The Box details several etiologies of adrenal insufficiency. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the leading cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in Western countries, with an estimated prevalence of 100 to 140 cases per million.1,2 Initial evaluation of patients with possible hypocortisolemia consists of an unstimulated morning (6:00-10:00 am) serum cortisol test (serum gel or red-top tube processed within 2 hours of collection; Medicare fee, $22.21) followed by a confirmatory 250-μg corticotropin stimulation test. Although reference range thresholds for morning cortisol values vary depending on the assay, a recent meta-analysis found that a morning cortisol level of less than 5 μg/dL (SI conversion to nmol/L, multiply by 27.588) best predicted adrenal insufficiency,3 while a cortisol level of greater than 13 μg/dL was usually consistent with normal adrenal function (area under the curve, 0.79 [95% CI, 0.75-0.82]).3,4 However, the Endocrine Society guidelines for primary adrenal insufficiency state that disagreement exists regarding unstimulated serum cortisol cutoffs.2 Higher thresholds for excluding adrenal insufficiency have been suggested, such as a value of 17 μg/dL, with levels between 5 and 17 μg/dL consistent with an equivocal result.2Adrenal (primary adrenal insufficiency; associated with elevated adrenocorticotropin hormone [ACTH])Infectious adrenalitis (eg, tuberculosis, AIDS, and fungal; second most common causes)Genetic causes (eg, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenoleukodystrophy, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome)Bilateral hemorrhage (eg, sepsis, trauma, antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulant use)Pituitary or hypothalamus (central adrenal insufficiency; associated with decreased ACTH and/or corticotropin-releasing hormone [CRH])Genetic causes (eg, mutations in proopiomelanocortin [POMC], T-box transcription factor [TPIT], paired-like homeobox 1 [PROP1])Inhibitors of cortisol synthesis (eg, etomidate, ketoconazole, metyrapone, mitotane)Other (eg, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, megestrol, cytoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 [CTLA-4], programmed death 1 [PD-1] inhibitors)Error in technique collection, processing, or both (appropriate collection should be in a serum gel or red-top tube and processed within 2 hours of collection)In a patient with hypotension, nausea, or vomiting, adrenal crisis should be suspected and immediate therapy with an appropriate stress dose glucocorticoid (typically hydrocortisone, 50 mg every 8 hours or equivalent) should be started while diagnostic test results are pending.2The following considerations are important when interpreting serum cortisol results. First, the serum cortisol assay measures total cortisol, which does not represent the biologically active free cortisol levels in conditions that cause cortisol-binding globulin deficiency (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, or critical illness) or cortisol-binding globulin excess (obesity, pregnancy, or oral contraceptives). Second, serum cortisol should not be measured to evaluate adrenal insufficiency in a patient taking glucocorticoids because most, except dexamethasone, crossreact with the assay.2 The morning cortisol level in a patient taking dexamethasone may be appropriately suppressed causing a false-positive test result for adrenal insufficiency. However, in these patients, the corticotropin stimulation test results are normal unless the patient was exposed to dexamethasone for several weeks or has primary adrenal insufficiency.A low morning serum cortisol level and an elevated adrenocorticotropin hormone level (ACTH >2-fold above the upper limit of the reference interval) support the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency.2 Skin hyperpigmentation is present in primary but not central adrenal insufficiency. Confirmation with the 250-μg corticotropin stimulation test should be performed in all suspected cases; baseline serum cortisol is drawn before the administration of 250 μg corticotropin intravenously or intramuscularly, and serum cortisol is drawn 30 to 60 minutes later.2 The patient’s corticotropin stimulation test showed cortisol values of less than 1 μg/dL at 30 and 60 minutes after stimulation, confirming primary adrenal insufficiency. Peak cortisol levels of greater than 18 μg/dL at 30 or 60 minutes indicate normal adrenal function (sensitivity, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.81-0.97]; specificity not available).5 Individuals with a seemingly low morning cortisol level (<5 μg/dL) may have normal adrenal function and have an increase in cortisol to greater than 18 μg/dL after the corticotropin stimulation test,6 as seen in the early phases of central adrenal insufficiency, since there has not been time for adrenal atrophy to occur. Initiation of glucocorticoid replacement therapy (usually at a total daily hydrocortisone maintenance dose of 15-30 mg or equivalent, administered 2 or 3 times daily) and referral to a specialist is advised for these patients.What Are Alternatives to an Initial Screening Test With Morning Cortisol Level?Serum free cortisol measurement is not readily available but may be helpful for diagnosing adrenal insufficiency when high or low cortisol-binding globulin levels exist. A coexisting mineralocorticoid deficiency is present in more than 95% of primary adrenal insufficiency cases. Elevated renin and low aldosterone levels may confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency early in the disease process, even before changes in cortisol or ACTH values occur. A dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (an adrenal androgen) value below the lower limit of normal for age and sex is a useful initial test of adrenal insufficiency when combined with morning cortisol measurement.2 None of these tests can reliably diagnose adrenal insufficiency. question: A 66-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of fevers, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash on the extensor surfaces of his lower and upper extremities. There were no other associated symptoms, including dyspnea, cough, urinary tract symptoms, or gastrointestinal symptoms.His medical history was significant for hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis. He was started on azathioprine for autoimmune hepatitis at a dose of 75 mg 10 days prior to his presentation after thiopurine methyltransferase activity was found to be normal. His other regular medications include aspirin, metformin, verapamil, and pravastatin.Examination was remarkable for a temperature of 38°C, an exquisitely tender erythematous papulonodular rash on the extensor surface of his lower and upper limbs, and bilaterally tender knees with a patellar tap (Figure 1). Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 10 500/μL (with neutrophil level elevated at 9900/μL [94%]) and elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein level, 76 mg/L [724 nmol/L]; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 69 mm/h). Rheumatoid factor was slightly elevated at 16 IU/mL, but testing for anti–citrullinated protein antibody was negative. Tests for double-stranded DNA, extractable nuclear antibodies, and anti-antistreptolysin O were negative. Renal function was normal, and there were no leukocytes, nitrates, red cells, or casts noted in the urine. Chest radiograph was also normal. Synovial fluid analysis showed a noninflammatory picture with a leukocyte count of 700 cells/L; no bacteria or crystals were seen.Tender erythematous papulonodular lesions on extensor surfaces of lower (left) and upper (right) extremities. explanation: The key to the diagnosis in this case is presence of a rash after administration of azathioprine, which, given the timing of the onset, represents a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the drug. Discontinuation of azathioprine is the best initial step.Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels are neither sensitive nor specific enough to be used for the diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Skin biopsy is usually diagnostic of erythema nodosum but only needed in atypical cases in which lesions spare the lower limbs or when tuberculosis is suspected and caseating granulomas are evident on histology. When performed, it is crucial to obtain a deep incisional biopsy. Punch biopsies frequently produce inadequate samples for a pathologic diagnosis.1 Glucocorticoids are not necessary in the majority of erythema nodosum cases, and corticosteroids may cause a worsening of already difficult to control diabetes.Erythema nodosum is the most common variant of panniculitis, occurring most often in persons aged 20 to 30 years.2 It is a painful disorder of the subcutaneous fat that is believed to represent a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to multiple antigens and frequently occurs in association with granulomatous disease.3 It most commonly is idiopathic or related to an upper respiratory tract infection.4 A variety of infectious agents can cause erythema nodosum such as bacterial (including streptococcus, tuberculosis, and brucellosis), viral (such as cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and herpes simplex virus), fungal (such as aspergillosis and histoplasmosis), and protozoal infections. Drugs have also been long recognized as a cause of erythema nodosum, including antibiotics (such as sulphonamides), antiepileptics, and oral contraceptive pills.5 Erythema nodosum in association with azathioprine hypersensitivity has been described.4 The reactive antigen is probably a thiopurine metabolite, as rechallenging with 6-mercaptopurine produces a similar hypersensitivity.5 Multiple other conditions can cause erythema nodosum, including sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, Behçet syndrome, pregnancy, and malignancy. Autoantibodies found in autoimmune hepatitis can also induce erythema nodosum, and this has been described6; however, it is very rare, and given the temporal relationship in this case of erythema nodosum onset with azathioprine, autoimmune hepatitis in itself is less likely to be the cause in this patient.Erythema nodosum presents with the acute onset of multiple symmetrical nonulcerating extremely painful subcutaneous nodules of the extremities. question: A woman in her 50s with a history of Crohn disease (CD) was referred for evaluation of painful perianal skin growths. The growths had been present for 1 year. Physical examination revealed a tender perianal plaque with a papular, cobblestone-like surface (Figure, A). She was taking no medications and had not had active gastrointestinal symptoms of CD in several years. A biopsy specimen from the perianal plaque was obtained (Figure, B and C).A, Multiple flesh-colored perianal papules and a pebbly plaque in a middle-aged woman with Crohn disease. B, A biopsy specimen of the perianal plaque was obtained, and histopathology revealed a dermal perivascular and nodular infiltrate composed of aggregates of histiocytes and (C) numerous multinucleate giant cells surrounded by mature lymphocytes. Acid-fast and silver stains were negative (not shown). What Is Your Diagnosis?

diagnosis: C. Granulomatous manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease
answer: Granulomatous manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease
explanation: Histopathological examination reveals a polypoid lesion with a perivascular and nodular dermal infiltrate (Figure, B). High-power magnification reveals discrete granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleate giant cells rimmed by mature lymphocytes (Figure, C). The patient had a history of CD but had not had evidence of active gastrointestinal disease for several years. The perianal granulomatous skin tag–like papules caused pain, bleeding, and hygiene problems that negatively affected her quality of life. Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 20 mg/mL in the cobblestone-appearing plaques effectively eliminated the lesions after 4 monthly treatments. Excision of the hypertrophic skin tags provided symptom relief.Perianal findings are common manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), especially in CD. In fact, perianal skin tags can be a clue to distinguish CD from ulcerative colitis in a young female patient with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea.1 Perianal manifestations of CD include abscesses, fissures, fistula, stenosis, and hypertrophic skin tags. Risk factors associated with perianal complications in established CD include patients younger than 40 years, nonwhite race, Sephardic Jewish ancestry, and colonic CD involvement.2 Certain genes (eg, TRAF3IP and PSTPIP1) have also been associated with an increased risk of perianal manifestations of CD.3,4 Symptoms can vary from anal discomfort to bleeding and pain, and can be associated with significant morbidity and poor quality of life.Cutaneous manifestations of CD can be divided into 3 categories: nutritional deficiency–associated dermatoses, reactive dermatoses, and cutaneous granulomatous disease.5 Biopsy of the lesion helps differentiate between the 3 categories. Cutaneous granulomatous disease can manifest along the gastrointestinal tract (perianal sites and oral mucosa) or in skin tissue and subcutaneous tissue at sites distal from gastrointestinal lesions (also known at metastatic CD). Cutaneous manifestations of CD vary widely among different populations. However, granulomatous perianal skin lesions are among the most common dermatologic manifestations of CD and have been reported to affect up to 53% of patients with CD.6 Nutritional deficiency–associated dermatoses related to malabsorption include entities such as acrodermatitis enteropathica and pellagra. Reactive cutaneous manifestations include conditions such as pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, oral aphthae, Sweet syndrome, and palmar erythema.7 Proper recognition and categorization of perianal findings in CD are crucial in aiding in the diagnosis, determining disease severity, and treatment selection.Biopsy specimen analysis is essential for diagnosing cutaneous lesions in CD. Histopathology of the perianal papules in this patient revealed a polypoid lesion with a dermal perivascular and nodular infiltrate composed of aggregates of histiocytes (granulomas) with numerous multinucleate giant cells surrounded by mature lymphocytes (Figure, B and C). These papules are, therefore, a granulomatous manifestation of IBD. In contrast, tissue biopsy of a fibroepithelial polyp would demonstrate a polypoid lesion with normal or slightly increased collagen, small-caliber vessels, and adipose tissue without granulomata. External hemorrhoids are composed of dilated, congested submucosal vessels with a squamous epithelial lining. Histopathologic examination of condyloma acuminatum would typically reveal acanthosis, mild papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis, with koilocytes (vacuolated keratinocytes with shrunken nuclei) that suggest viropathic change.Controlling the underlying disease may result in improvement of granulomatous skin lesions in CD; however, cutaneous and gastrointestinal disease course and response to treatment do not always correlate. In the case of our patient, the granulomatous skin tag–like papules caused pain, bleeding, and hygiene problems that negatively affected her quality of life despite quiescent disease activity of her intestinal IBD. There are reports in the literature documenting the successful treatment of cutaneous manifestations of IBD with conventional immunosuppressants and anti–tumor necrosis factor agents. We decided to treat with intralesional steroids for the plaque in an attempt to reduce the risk of potential adverse effects associated with systemic agents given the absence of active intestinal disease in our patient. There was near complete resolution of the cobblestoned plaque after 4 monthly treatments, and then excision of the residual pedunculated papules was performed.Early recognition and categorization of perianal manifestations of IBD helps guide therapy that will reduce overall morbidity in affected patients. A better recognition of these skin manifestations by dermatologist can help guide management.8

question: A man in his early 40s with a medical history significant for verruca vulgaris, dyshidrotic eczema, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) diagnosed 1 year prior to presentation reported a chief complaint of dry, swollen lips. The patient reported a 1-month history of “puffy and bumpy” lips. He also described his lower lip as sometimes becoming “dry and scaly” during this time but denied any bleeding from the area. On physical examination, there were several erythematous papules at the vermillion border of the lower lip within a background of edema (Figure, A and B). In addition, the patient had slight fissuring of the tongue, but the remainder of the oral mucosa was normal and intact. Findings of a complete review of systems were unremarkable, other than occasional headaches. The patient denied fevers, night sweats, abdominal pain, neurologic symptoms, chest pain, cough, and shortness of breath. He disclosed full compliance with his HIV highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which included ritonavir, darunavir, etravirine, and raltegravir. He also reported taking sumatriptan as needed for headaches. Numerous laboratory tests were performed, including a complete blood cell count, complete metabolic panel, CD4 count, HIV viral load, and assays for C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and rapid plasma reagin; all results were normal except for a slightly elevated angiotensin converting enzyme level (84 µg/L; normal, 9-67 µg/L). His CD4 count was within normal limits (520 cells/µL) and HIV viral load was undetectable. A biopsy was performed on the right lower lip (Figure, C and D).Clinical images (A and B) show persistent, nontender swelling of the lips in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus, showing erythematous papules at the vermillion border and edema of the lower lip. C and D, Histologic images of a biopsy specimen from a papule on the lower lip show, at low magnification (C), a nodular, nonnecrotizing granulomatous dermatitis and, at higher magnification (D), the presence of epithelioid histiocytes with admixed lymphocytes. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: The biopsy specimen showed nodular, nonnecrotizing granulomatous dermatitis most consistent with granulomatous cheilitis (Figure, C). Higher-power magnification (Figure, D) demonstrated the presence of epithelioid histiocytes with admixed lymphocytes. The lack of well-formed granulomas disfavors the diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid. In addition, thorough examination of the patient’s skin and eyes revealed no other findings consistent with sarcoidosis, and a recent chest radiograph showed nothing remarkable. The patient was treated with topical corticosteroid cream, but returned to clinic 3 months later with minimal improvement in his symptoms. Other treatment options, including intralesional corticosteroids, tetracyclines, and hydroxychloroquine, were discussed with him at that time.Granulomatous cheilitis is characterized as a nontender chronic swelling of the lips.1 Also known as Miescher cheilitis, it is considered a manifestation of orofacial granulomatosis, a clinical term used to describe orofacial swelling caused by noninfectious, nonnecrotizing granulomatous disorders of the lips and face in the absence of systemic disease. It is a rare disorder that primarily affects young adults but can occur at any age and has no predisposition to race, sex, or age. Many factors have been speculated to contribute in the disease process, including genetic susceptibility, atopy, and infections.2 There have also been previous reports of patients with HIV undergoing HAART therapy who have subsequently developed granulomatous cheilitis.3,4 However, as with most cases of granulomatous cheilitis, the relationship has not been proven to be causal, and the disease is often characterized as idiopathic with no clear etiology.Patients will usually be asymptomatic early in the disease process, typically complaining only of intermittent swelling of the lips. The swelling can be isolated to the upper or lower lip but can also affect both lips simultaneously. In most cases, granulomatous cheilitis is an isolated finding; however, it is not uncommon to see fissuring of the tongue. Also, though exceedingly rare, it has been reported to be associated with facial nerve palsy, otherwise known as Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome.5 As the disease progresses, the frequency and duration of attacks increase until the symptoms become persistent.6 This can result in functional impairment and severe cosmetic disfigurement, both of which can significantly reduce a person’s quality of life.Lip biopsy is often necessary for the diagnosis and can assist in ruling out other diseases with similar oral involvement, such as angioedema, oral sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, or infections. Typically, histologic analysis will show scattered, small noncaseating granulomas containing epithelioid histiocytes. However, it must be noted that granulomatous inflammation is not always present, especially early in the disease process, and histologic analysis might show only edema and perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells. Therefore, the diagnosis of granulomatous cheilitis is frequently one of exclusion.As reviewed by Banks et al,7 treatment of granulomatous cheilitis has proven to be a very difficult task and highly unpredictable. Depending on the patient, response to treatment is highly variable, and complete remission is uncommon. Multiple therapies, used alone or in combination, have been reported to show some efficacy in individual patients. Some of these include topical, intralesional, and systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, and immunomodulators. Patients with severe and refractory cases that fail to respond to conservative medical management may benefit from surgical excision of excess tissue.8

question: Six years ago, a white woman in her 60s was incidentally found to have chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) after being noticed to have lymphocytosis during treatment for diverticulitis. Immunophenotyping was typical for CLL, showing expression of CD 5, CD 19, CD 23, CD 38, and dim κ light chain restriction. However, 2.5 years later she experienced disease relapse. Repeated cytogenetic tests showed complex karyotype with del(17)(p13.1) in 35% of her cells as a new abnormality. The immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgHV) gene mutational status was studied at this time and found to be unmutated, with somatic mutation rate of 0%. How Do You Interpret These Test Results?

explanation: During normal B-cell development, the variable region of IgHV genes goes through V-D-J rearrangement to generate a diverse B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire. Furthermore, on antigen stimulation, somatic hypermutation in the rearranged IgHV regions occurs in the germinal center of lymph nodes (GC phase), a process that further modifies the BCR’s affinity for antigens. Therefore, like normal B cells, all CLL cells have unique VDJ rearranged IgHV genes that can be used as specific clonal markers. However, only about half of patients with CLL have somatic hypermutation in the IgHV region of their tumor cells. Whether the CLL clone has somatic hypermutation within the IgHV gene is likely to indicate if the tumor precursor cells had gone through the GC phase before transformation.This analysis of IgHV mutational status is performed by comparing the gene sequences from CLL cells with the sequences from somatic cells. The cutoff value to define mutation status was generally set to a greater than 2% difference to rule out polymorphisms and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) errors. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia cases with 1% to 2% mutations have been reported to contain true somatic mutations, but these CLL cases with low levels of mutation seem to have a prognosis similar to that of unmutated cases. IgHV mutation status does not change over time in a given patient.IgHV mutational status is a very important prognostic factor, with unmutated cases (U-CLL) having considerably lower median time to first treatment (TTFT), chemoimmunotherapy response duration, and overall survival (OS) when compared with mutated cases (M-CLL).1,2 However, the response rate and complete response (CR) rate to chemotherapy regiments (eg, FR and fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab [FCR]) are not different between U-CLL and M-CLL.3The worst prognosis in U-CLL cases is likely to be related to both the enrichment of genetic abnormalities that confer higher aggressiveness and poorer clinical outcome (eg, mutations of NOTCH1, SF3B1, BIRC3, and p53). Unmutated CLL clones are also more likely to undergo clonal evolution and to acquire high-risk cytogenetic features, such as del(17)(p13.1) deletion or complex karyotype. Patients with U-CLL are also at higher risk of Richter transformation.Application of the Test Result to This PatientIgHV mutational status is a useful clinical test at the time of diagnosis and also when assessing what to treat the patient with when symptoms developed. The patient described herein was found to have IgHV U-CLL at a later time in her disease course. IgHV mutational status is usually stable and does not change over time in a patient along the course of disease progression.At diagnosis, approximately 40% of patients will have U-CLL with a more aggressive course that includes shorter TTFT and OS. Identification of U-CLL does not change the typical treatment approach to asymptomatic CLL, that being observation until progression. However, it does allow patients to know what the future holds to permit planning. It also empowers patients by allowing them to know more about their disease. The patient described herein indeed had a rapidly progressing absolute lymphocyte count and lymphadenopathy on diagnosis, requiring treatment within 6 months of first diagnosis.At the time of first treatment, approximately 60% of all patients with CLL who require first treatment will have U-CLL, reflecting the increased propensity for this genomic group to develop progressive disease. With the recent plethora of new therapeutics and changing landscape of CLL therapy, IgHV mutational status is one of the most useful tests in our current practice. Unmutated-CLL does not predict initial response to chemoimmunotherapy but does predict faster relapse after therapy, which occurs in virtually all patients. This contrasts with individuals with IgHV-mutated disease who can have prolonged (>10-year) remissions after chemoimmunotherapy with FCR. In our current practice, we consider chemoimmunotherapy (FCR) options for symptomatic patients with IgHV mutation when appropriate because they have the potential to induce very durable remissions. In contrast, those with U-CLL do not attain durable remissions with chemoimmunotherapy and are predisposed to clonal evolution and a higher frequency of Richter transformation. Our approach is to direct these patients to non–chemotherapy-based immune or targeted therapies, ideally as part of a clinical trial. The patient described herein followed the expected pattern, having initially achieved CR after 4 cycles of FR but relapsing only 2.5 years later. In addition, she demonstrated clonal evolution, going from a favorable cytogenetic profile at treatment (single 13q deletion) but at relapse had acquisition of del(17) (p13.1) and complex karyotype. Fortunately, new targeted therapies, such as ibrutinib, have shown promising results on these poor-risk patients with CLL and may change the landscape of CLL treatment.Although widely available now, in the past, sequencing of the IgHV region was difficult to obtain for routine clinical practice. This prompted search for potential surrogate prognostic factors often examined by flow cytometry. One is CD38 expression, a flow cytometry–based test with faster turnover rate. CD38 positivity (defined as >30% positive cells) has been shown to correlate with unmutated IgHV genes and has an independent prognostic value.2 However, although M-CLL cases usually show low levels of CD38, U- CLL cases can have a wide range of CD38 expression levels. Also, unlike IgHV gene mutation status, which remains stable overtime, the levels of CD38 may change during disease progression. Another factor, CD49d expression, has also shown promise as a predictor of rapid disease progression at the time of initial diagnosis.4 Most characterized and controversial for this purpose is ZAP-70, a protein that is typically expressed in T cells but not B cells. IgHV U-CLL cells are associated with considerably higher level of ZAP-70 messenger RNA (mRNA) and protein expression. ZAP-70 expression in CLL cells enhances BCR signaling and therefore affects leukemia cell proliferation and interaction with the microenvironment. ZAP-70 expression predicts shorter time to treatment and OS. In contrast to CD38 and CD49d, ZAP-70 expression levels tend not to change over time.5 A limiting factor of ZAP-70 is that it is an intracellular protein, which makes the flow cytometry testing difficult to standardize. Also, it is not stable, and time to procession also affects the result. Methylation analysis of the DNA sequence CpG+223 from exon 1 of the ZAP-70 gene has been shown to correlate well with both mRNA and protein expression. Unmethylated CPG+223 predicts poorer OS and shorter time to treatment. Methylation analysis is more reproducible and provides superior prognostic information compared with checking ZAP-70 protein expression.6The patient started ibrutinib on a clinical trial 3 years ago and responded well to the treatment with minimal adverse effects. She had resolution of lymphadenopathy and symptoms, and the CLL cells almost disappeared from peripheral blood (only about 0.1% of peripheral lymphocytes). A bone marrow biopsy only showed a minute κ light chain–restricted clonal CD19+/CD5+ B cell population.IgHV mutational status is an important prognostic factor in chronic lymphocytic leukemia .The cutoff value to define mutation status was generally set to a greater than 2% difference to rule out polymorphisms and polymerase chain reaction errors.IgHV unmutated cases predict poor clinical outcome, with lower median survival and more aggressive clinical course,Patients with an IgHV mutation can have very prolonged durable remissions with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.IgHV unmutated cases are enriched with other high-risk features, such as NOTCH1, SF3B1, BIR3, and p53 mutation/deletion, and stimulated complex karyotype.IgHV unmutated cases are at higher risk of clonal evolution, acquisition of new cytogenetic abnormalities, and Richter transformation.

question: An 18-year-old man presented with an upper respiratory tract infection that persisted for a week without improvement. Because of this infection, he went to an emergency department and was prescribed antibiotics for presumed sinusitis. Five days later, he developed painless horizontal diplopia and returned to the emergency department. Findings from a computed tomographic scan showed diffuse sinusitis that was procedurally drained by an otolaryngologist. However, this treatment did not resolve the diplopia and he was subsequently referred to a neurologist. Additional evaluation included a repeated computed tomographic scan that showed no infectious involvement of the orbits or petromastoid complexes (Figure). Findings from magnetic resonance imaging of the patient’s brain and orbits did not reveal intracranial lesions or extraocular muscle myositis. Results of lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid testing, including opening pressure, cell count, and glucose and protein levels, were in the reference range. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels were also in the reference range. Findings from neurologic examination did not reveal paresthesias, difficulty with gait, or abnormal tendon reflexes.A, A computed tomographic scan of the face and orbits in coronal sections demonstrating inflammatory changes in the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses without orbital involvement. B, An axial computed tomographic scan does not show inflammatory involvement of the petrous apices (digitally processed image). A indicates anterior.The patient was then referred for neuro-ophthalmic evaluation. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. Positive findings were limited to a −2.5 bilateral abduction deficit. Alternate cover testing revealed a 30 prism diopters (∆) esotropia on primary gaze that increased to 45∆ on lateral gaze. His pupils, intraocular pressure, visual fields, and findings from external examination were normal. Findings from anterior segment and dilated fundus examinations were also normal. The angle of esotropia was not improved with a 30-minute sleep test.Restart antibiotic treatment and arrange for an otorhinolaryngology follow-up examination What Would You Do Next?

explanation: Results from the patient’s laboratory tests revealed positive anti-GQ1b autoantibodies consistent with the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome. In addition to external ophthalmoplegia, the classic triad of Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) includes ataxia and loss of tendon reflexes.1,2 The latter 2 features, however, were absent in our patient. This relatively milder presentation of MFS was described by Yuki and colleagues3,4 as acute ophthalmoparesis (AO), which typically presents with an external ophthalmoplegia without ataxia or marked paresis of the limbs and facial muscles. Patients may also have blepharoptosis, mild facial weakness, and abnormal tendon reflexes. However, an isolated ophthalmoplegia was the only presenting sign in 3 of 21 patients in a case series of patients with AO.3 The pattern of ophthalmoplegia is variable and can include deficits of both horizontal and vertical gaze. While the gaze deficit is usually bilateral, it can be unilateral in about one-fourth of patients. The most common pattern of ophthalmoplegia, however, is a bilateral abduction deficit, which is observed in about one-third of patients with AO.2,3,5Antibodies to the GQ1b ganglioside are present in about 85% to 90% of MFS cases during the acute phase of illness.1,2,6 Antibody titers in patients with AO are similar to those of patients with typical MFS.3 In a case series of patients with AO, symptoms of an antecedent infection, such as an upper respiratory tract illness or gastroenteritis, were present in 81% of patients before the onset of ophthalmoparesis.3 The ophthalmoparesis of AO and MFS typically occurs within 3 weeks of experiencing an antecedent infection. Campylobacter jejuni is the most familiar organism described in association with MFS and AO; it has been shown to express a molecule on its membrane surface that is structurally similar to the GQ1b-like gangliosides found in human tissue.7 By molecular mimicry, exposure and sensitization to the microbial GQ1b epitope leads to production of the autoantibodies that are responsible for AO and MFS.1,2,6 The predilection for AO and MFS to involve the extraocular muscles is explained by the asymmetric distribution of GQ1b-like gangliosides in different human nerve and muscle tissues. Results from immunohistochemical evaluations have shown a greater abundance of GQ1b-like gangliosides in extraocular muscles compared with skeletal muscle elsewhere.6While there are no established guidelines for the treatment of AO, prior published cases2-5 have adopted strategies used in managing MFS and Guillain-Barré syndrome, including plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin treatment. Because systemic corticosteroids are not helpful in treating some more common variants of Guillain-Barré syndrome,7 their use in treating AO is not advised.2,3 As with our patient, spontaneous recovery can occur without the need for intervention.1-3,5 When we were notified of the positive results of GQ1b autoantibody testing, the patient had reported symptomatic improvement that corresponded to a reduction in his degree of esotropia; a decision was then made to forego plasmapheresis.Although the patient’s clinical course would have remained the same if observation alone was chosen, the diagnosis would likely have been missed without appropriate serum testing. In addition to MFS, screening for autoantibodies can help evaluate entities such as the systemic vasculitides. The antecedent sinusitis in our patient involved classic symptoms of AO, but the severity of disease, which required surgical drainage, should raise concern for Gradenigo syndrome.8  However, the patient did not have otitis media or involvement of the petrous or mastoid bones (Figure). Magnetic resonance venography may have been an appropriate choice if the patient had an elevated cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure and other signs and symptoms of central venous sinus thrombosis, such as headaches, focal neurologic deficits, or seizures.9 The negative result on the sleep test added evidence against the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.The patient’s condition continued to improve but he was unavailable for follow-up. There was vitreous hemorrhage with a poor view of the posterior pole (Figure, A).A, Ultra-widefield fundus photograph of the left eye showing posterior vitreous hemorrhage (white arrowhead) and a choroidal detachment temporally (yellow arrowheads). Tortuosity of the temporal vessels was prominent, with diffuse peripheral vascular leakage temporally. Choroidal folds were observed 3 disc diameters temporal to the macula, extending to the periphery. diagnosis: Waldenström macroglobulinemia with bilateral choroidal detachment
answer: Treat with combined systemic chemotherapy and pars plana vitrectomy
explanation: Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a rare lymphoplasmacytic malignant lymphoma characterized by the overproduction of monoclonal IgM.1 The clinical manifestations of WM are classified according to those related to the following 3 causes: direct tumor infiltration, the amount and specific properties of circulating IgM, and the deposition of IgM in various tissues. Because IgM is a large pentamer compound that easily forms aggregates, elevated serum IgM levels in WM can cause hyperviscosity syndrome, leading to ocular manifestations. Most known ophthalmic manifestations, including retinal hemorrhages, peripheral retinal capillary nonperfusion, macular detachment, and central retinal vein occlusion, have been linked to hyperviscosity syndrome because of WM.2 Other characteristic retinal findings caused by high viscosity in patients with WM are microaneurysms, vascular dilation and tortuosity, venous beading, and optic disc edema. Approximately 30% of all patients with WM develop chorioretinal complications.2 Patients may experience visual disturbance (8%) and may exhibit some degree of hyperviscosity-related retinopathy (37%),3 which can lead to central retinal vein occlusion, peripheral nonperfusion, retinal hemorrhage,3,4 and central serous macular detachment.5 We describe a patient with WM who developed bilateral choroidal detachment, which, to our knowledge, has not been previously reported. The precise mechanism underlying the choroidal alterations in WM remains poorly understood. The microvasculature of the retina and choroid are particularly susceptible to the effects of serum hyperviscosity.6 It is possible that increased IgM in choroidal vessels spills and leaks into the suprachoroidal space. The high molecular weight of IgM may have increased the fluid oncotic pressure within the suprachoroidal space and hence resulted in fluid transudation and choroidal detachment in this patient with WM.This report also describes wide-field fundus photography and fluorescein angiography for visualization of peripheral fundus findings, including peripheral vascular leakage, capillary nonperfusion, vascular remodeling, and neovascularization. The patient did not have diabetes mellitus or sickle cell disease, thereby ruling out some other known causes of peripheral vascular ischemia or leakage. B-scan ultrasonography was helpful in delineating the extent and height of detachment in the left eye and detecting the small choroidal detachment in the right eye, which was not readily seen on clinical examination.For our patient, chemotherapy was initiated for the reactivated WM. She underwent pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser in the left eye and vision in that eye improved to 20/20, with resolution of the choroidal detachment at the 1-month follow-up.

question: A man in his mid-20s with a history of alcohol abuse presented with abdominal pain after 3 days of drinking. He described the pain as a sharp, left upper-quadrant pain migrating to the epigastric region for 24 hours. The patient had a history of multiple episodes of hematemesis attributed to alcoholic gastritis; however, at this admission, he indicated he had not experienced vomiting. He admitted to early satiety over the past few months. Physical examination revealed a soft nondistended abdomen, but it was very tender in the epigastric region without rebound or guarding. There was no palpable mass. Elevated results of liver function tests, as well as amylase and lipase levels consistent with alcoholic pancreatitis, were noted. Magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomographic imaging, and upper endoscopy findings are shown in Figure 1. Biopsy results of the mass were reported as normal gastric mucosa.Diagnostic imaging. A, Computed tomographic scan and magnetic resonance imaging (inset) demonstrating a heterogeneous mass lesion in the fundus and body of the stomach. B, Upper endoscopic image directly visualizing the mass intruding into the lumen of the stomach. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Initial abdominal and pelvic computed tomographic and magnetic resonance imaging studies demonstrated a large (9.8 × 7.4 × 7.6-cm) heterogeneous mass located in the fundus and body of the stomach with areas of enhancement, suspicious for a possible gastrointestinal stromal tumor. On upper endoscopy, the mass occupied the upper half of the stomach, including the gastroesophageal junction, but did not extend proximally into the esophagus. Specimens obtained during progressively deeper biopsies on 2 successive occasions revealed no pathologic diagnosis.Preoperatively, endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration biopsy was considered.1 ,2 Social issues prevented the patient from undergoing this test. The mass was surgically resected for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The patient recovered well postoperatively and was discharged home on hospital day 8. Final pathology examination revealed this lesion to be composed of stomach duplication tissue, confirming a diagnosis of gastric duplication cyst (Figure 2).Gross pathologic examination of the specimen demonstrates a noncommunicating gastric duplication cyst. The inset demonstrates gastric mucosal lining on either side of the gastric duplication wall (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×20).Gastrointestinal duplication cysts are a rare congenital anomaly, accounting for approximately 4% of all intestinal duplications. 3 ,4 In 1959, Rowling5  proposed 3 morphologic criteria for the correct diagnosis of gastric duplication cysts: first, the cyst must be contiguous with the stomach wall; second, the cyst must be surrounded by at least 1 coat of smooth muscle, fusing with muscularis propria of the stomach; and third, the cyst must be lined with typical gastric mucosa. Figure 2 depicts normal gastric mucosa, a common muscularis, and attenuated gastric mucosa of the duplication on the right. The clinical presentation generally includes bowel obstruction or gastrointestinal bleeding early in life; torsion, hemorrhage, pancreatitis, and fistula formation may also occur.3,5-8 Rarely does gastric duplication present in adulthood.9 Malignant transformation has been identified in patients with gastric duplication; thus, complete resection is recommended at the time of diagnosis.10There was an associated small, noncommunicating esophageal duplication as noted. Findings at surgery included a large proximal gastric mass fibrotically adherent to the diaphragm in a desmoplastic and presumed neoplastic fashion. Total gastrectomy with removal of adherent diaphragm was undertaken with Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy. We believe the chronic, unopposed acid production within the excluded gastric remnant led to full-thickness ulceration, perforation, and adherence of the stomach to the diaphragm and retroperitoneum.

question: A 28-year-old white man presented to the gastrointestinal (GI) medicine clinic for persistent nausea and vomiting. He had a long-standing history of gastroesophageal reflux disease that was only partially controlled with proton pump inhibitor therapy. The symptoms were exacerbated by cessation of proton pump inhibitor medication, and he reported an associated 9-kg weight loss. Results of laboratory testing were significant for iron deficiency anemia (hematocrit, 31% [to convert to proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01]) and hemeoccult-positive stool. Upper and lower endoscopy, computed tomography enterography, PillCam capsule endoscopy, and a Meckel scan failed to identify a source of GI bleeding. The patient received a retrograde double-balloon enteroscopy that showed an outpouching in the distal ileum (Figure, A) with an accompanying ulceration of the adjacent mucosa (Figure, B). Exploratory laparotomy with small-bowel resection was performed, and the gross specimen is shown in Figure, C.A, Outpouching of the distal ileum. B, Ulceration adjacent to the outpouching of the distal ileum. C, Resected distal ileum revealing an ulceration of the mucosa. Arrowhead indicates site of ulceration. What Is the Diagnosis?
explanation: The retrograde double-balloon enteroscopy (Figure, A) demonstrated the diverticulum and small-bowel ulceration (Figure, B) secondary to acid secretion from ectopic gastric mucosa. The gross specimen (Figure, C) demonstrated the Meckel diverticulum (MD) located on the antimesenteric border and the ulcer in the ileum adjacent to the diverticulum (arrowhead). The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and has had complete resolution of symptoms at follow-up.Meckel diverticulum results from incomplete obliteration of the omphalomesenteric duct. The incidence is estimated between 1% and 2% in the population, and it is the most common congenital anomaly of the digestive tract.1 Some potential complications of MD include hemorrhage, obstruction, inflammation, perforation, or intussusception, with a 4% to 6% lifetime risk of these events.2 While most pediatric cases of MD present as intestinal obstruction, GI bleeding is the most common presentation in adults.3The diagnosis of MD is notoriously elusive owing to nonspecific symptoms and difficulty in disease detection, with technetium Tc 99m pertechnetate scintigraphy sensitivity estimated at 75%.4 Recent advances in endoscopic techniques, including double-balloon enteroscopy, have improved the ability to identify the sources of occult GI bleeding, with one study quoting a diagnostic yield of 80.6%.5 Double-balloon enteroscopy was pioneered in 2001 by Yamamoto and colleagues6 and uses a thin endoscope and soft overtube, both equipped with latex balloons. With both balloons inflated, the overtube and endoscope can be concurrently withdrawn, creating an accordion effect within the bowel that allows for advancement of the endoscope through the overtube. Subsequent inflation and deflation of the balloons is repeated until visualization of the entire small bowel has been achieved.Bleeding associated with MD is most frequently due to peptic ulceration of the small-bowel mucosa adjacent to heterotopic gastric mucosa within the diverticulum. This point highlights the importance of inspecting the surgical specimen to ensure the ulceration is included in the specimen. Failure to do so may result in continued bleeding. Meckel diverticulum is an important part of the differential diagnosis of occult GI bleeding in adults, and double-balloon enteroscopy may be a useful diagnostic tool.

question: A 21-year-old college student presents for evaluation of an intensely pruritic eruption on the ankle and sole of his right foot. The patient recently returned from a trip to Puerto Rico. He noticed the lesions approximately 1 week after his return. He has no significant past medical history. On physical examination, the patient is in overall good health. Notable findings include 3 red, serpiginous lesions on the heel (Figure, A), lateral area of the midfoot (Figure, B), and ankle, some with vesicles. Vesicles were also noted over the Achilles tendon.Serpiginous lesions on the heel (A) and lateral area of the midfoot (B) of the patient. What Would You Do Next?
opa: Do nothing; it will resolve with time
explanation: The key clinical features of this case include the erythematous serpiginous lesions on the foot seen soon after returning from an endemic region. This presentation is typical for CLM.Cutaneous larva migrans is a common dermatosis acquired in tropical and subtropical countries.1 It is most commonly caused by the skin-penetrating larvae of the hookworm species Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, and Uncinaria stenocephala, found in infected cat or dog feces.2 When a human steps or sits on the larvae, the larvae can penetrate the epidermis. However, since the larvae cannot penetrate the basal layer of the epithelium, they remain within the epidermis.2 Although the larvae are unable to complete their life cycle in human epidermis and will die over time, the disease can, if untreated, persist for months and cause a pruritic eruption.2According to data from the GeoSentinel global surveillance network, CLM is the most common dermatologic disorder seen among patients returning from travel to specific regions.3 The endemic areas most commonly reported are (in descending order of frequency) Latin America and the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa.3 The condition is seen in those who walked barefoot at beaches where there are infected roaming animals.4 Because CLM is not a reportable disease in the United States, the number of human cases is unknown. However, many cases of CLM continue to be diagnosed in the United States, particularly in the southeastern states.5Itching with CLM generally begins soon after larval penetration.2  The patient may see a small reddish papule at the site of penetration. After a variable incubation period, the characteristic serpiginous, erythematous, slightly elevated track becomes visible (Figure, A). Vesicles and papules can be seen overlying the linear track.1 The intensity of the itching at this point is great and can cause sleep disturbance. In addition, scratching and excoriation can lead to bacterial superinfection.2 The larvae can migrate up to 1 centimeter every day. The actual location of the larvae within the epidermis is usually 1 to 2 cm beyond the advancing edge of the track, with implications as to where to biopsy.1Although CLM infection is self-limiting and generally resolves in approximately 1 to 3 months with resorption of the dead larvae, treatment is generally required because of the intense pruritus.4 First-line treatment for CLM is 1 dose of oral ivermectin (200 µg/kg).2 Some sources suggest the dose should be repeated the next day.6 Cure rates of large studies of single-dose ivermectin ranged from 77%7 to 95%.8 Pruritus resolved after an average of 3 days, and the creeping eruption after an average of 9 days.9 If there is no improvement after 10 days, a second dose can be administered.4 Second-line treatment is oral albendazole (400-800 mg/d for 3 days).5 Topical options include albendazole 10% used 3 times a day for 7 to 10 days4 as well as compounded thiabendazole 15% applied 3 times a day for 5 to 10 days, although thiabendazole can be difficult to obtain.9 Freezing the edges of the tracks is not recommended because the larvae are generally located beyond the visible end of the track. In addition, the procedure is painful and causes chronic ulcerations.5 Topical corticosteroids and antihistamines can be used in addition to the anthelmintic agents for symptomatic relief of pruritus.1The patient was initially seen by his university health service and diagnosed with contact dermatitis. He was given topical corticosteroids. After a week, he had little relief from the pruritus and was reevaluated and diagnosed with CLM. To ensure eradication of the patient’s infection and because the patient was returning to school and would not be available for follow-up, he was given two 15-mg doses of oral ivermectin. The patient reported that after approximately 24 hours he had relief from the pruritus. The tracks receded 7 to 10 days later.
