explanation: Intraocular lens (IOL) dislocation is an uncommon complication of cataract surgery, estimated to occur after 0.3% to 2.0% of cases.1,2 Risk factors for late postoperative IOL dislocation, defined as dislocation 3 or more months following surgery, include etiologies of zonular weakness such as pseudoexfoliation syndrome, retinitis pigmentosa, trauma, high myopia, prior vitreoretinal surgery, and connective tissue diseases.3 Investigations suggest 0.6% of patients with pseudophakia with these risk factors require corrective surgery for dislocations within 10 years of cataract surgery.2 Surgery typically is indicated for decreased visual acuity or lens dislocation-induced retinal detachment, glaucoma, or uveitis.4 Both IOL exchange and suture fixation are potential treatments.3This case involves unilateral PCIOL dislocation in a patient with −1.50 D myopia and no history of trauma, retinitis pigmentosa, or additional intraocular surgery. The etiology of dislocation should be considered before surgery is performed (choice A). Connective tissue diseases can be associated with juvenile cataracts and zonular weakness but are associated with extraocular manifestations, making them less likely in this patient.5 Pseudoexfoliation syndrome can be considered given the iris transillumination defects in the fellow eye, but these can also occur following intraocular surgery.The scleral pigmentation and subluxed IOL in the opposing direction make a ciliary body tumor a consideration. Specifically, the focality, elevation, and vascularity of the lesion are concerning. The lesion should be investigated further with imaging before a biopsy is performed (choice D). Optical coherence tomography is useful for conjunctival tumors but is limited in evaluating pathologies posterior to the iris (choice C). However, ultrasound biomicroscopy should provide a high-resolution image of the PCIOL position and evaluate for ciliary body masses, making choice B the correct answer. Indeed, ultrasound biomicroscopy identified a large ciliary mass displacing the PCIOL (Figure 2). B-scan ultrasonography revealed a large ciliochoroidal melanoma measuring 21 mm in largest basal diameter and 16 mm in thickness (Figure 2, inset). Systemic staging imaging did not reveal metastases.Ultrasound biomicroscopy demonstrating intraocular lens subluxation (pink arrowhead) by a ciliochoroidal melanoma (white arrowhead). Inset, B-scan ultrasound reveals the large intraocular mass.This case highlights that ciliary body masses may not be apparent until quite large. The intraocular melanoma was not seen at the time the subluxed IOL was initially identified. While most uveal melanomas are now treated with radiation therapy, enucleation is indicated for the largest tumors (largest basal diameter >20 mm, thickness >12 mm).6,7 Following primary treatment, patients with uveal melanoma undergo surveillance for both local and distant recurrence. Unfortunately, the risk for distant metastasis approaches 50% and is elevated with ciliary body location.6 There is currently no curative therapy for metastatic uveal melanoma.6,7Given the tumor size, enucleation of the right eye was performed. Pathology confirmed a mixed-type uveal melanoma. Six months after enucleation, liver metastases were identified, presumably related to presence of micrometastases at the time of initial diagnosis and treatment. Because of progressive disease despite immunotherapy, the patient transferred to hospice 1 year after treatment of the intraocular tumor.

The patient was nonverbal at baseline and exhibited restrictive and repetitive behaviors. His diet consisted exclusively of cookies, apples, potato chips, and Gatorade. Yellow or white punctate peripheral retinal lesions may be seen, indicating photoreceptor dysfunction. Pediatric idiopathic intracranial hypertension and nerve atrophy have also been associated with vitamin A deficiency.2,3 Children with ocular signs of vitamin A deficiency have reduced immunity and a higher mortality rate.3,4Children with ASD frequently have nutritional deficits owing to picky eating habits,5 which held true for this patient. His serum vitamin A level was very low at 3.58 μg/dL (normal range, 28.65-94.56 μg/dL ).6The most common ophthalmic symptom of vitamin A deficiency is nyctalopia secondary to rod photoreceptor dysfunction.3 This can be missed in children with ASD, as they may be unable to express difficulty seeing in the dark. explanation: The key to the diagnosis is the combination of cutaneous lesions characteristic of Sweet syndrome with constitutional symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss), pancytopenia, and acute DVT, which may be associated with hematologic malignancy. Incision and drainage (choice C) may result in worsening of the lesions in response to trauma (pathergy). Although oral dapsone (choice D) may be used as a steroid-sparing agent, it is not the recommended first-line treatment for Sweet syndrome.Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is an inflammatory noninfectious disorder characterized by the abrupt onset of painful erythematous skin plaques, nodules, or papules, often accompanied by fever, arthralgias, myalgias, and malaise.1 Patients with Sweet syndrome frequently have an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level. Skin biopsy, which is required for the diagnosis of Sweet syndrome, demonstrates a dense neutrophilic infiltrate without leukocytoclastic vasculitis.2Sweet syndrome is a rare condition that typically affects older adults,3 and its exact pathogenesis is unclear.4 The differential diagnosis includes infection (eg, erysipelas, secondary syphilis), eosinophilic dermatoses, malignancy (eg, leukemia cutis, cutaneous metastases), panniculitides (eg, erythema nodosum), and vasculidities (eg, polyarteritis nodosa).2 Evaluation for infection ideally includes fresh tissue culture and use of stains for organisms on fixed tissue.Classic Sweet syndrome may be preceded by a recent infection with a virus (eg, hepatitis C, HIV, SARS-CoV-2),5 nontuberculous myocbacteria,6 fungi, or bacteria.2 It has also been associated with inflammatory bowel disease,7 pregnancy, and autoimmune connective tissue disorders.2Approximately 20% of patients with Sweet syndrome have associated malignancy, most commonly acute myeloid leukemia and MDS.2 Evaluation for an underlying hematologic malignancy is recommended for patients who have Sweet syndrome and anemia.8 Sweet syndrome may precede, follow, or present concurrently with the diagnosis of malignancy.9 Recurrence of Sweet syndrome may herald relapse or progression of an underlying malignancy.10Drug-induced Sweet syndrome is temporally associated with ingestion of a medication3 and may recur with drug reexposure. The most common drugs associated with Sweet syndrome are granulocyte colony–stimulating factor, azathioprine, and all-trans retinoic acid.4The cutaneous and systemic symptoms of Sweet syndrome typically improve rapidly with initiation of systemic glucocorticoids, commonly oral prednisone (0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day). Indomethacin, acitretin, colchicine, and dapsone may be used as steroid-sparing agents if Sweet syndrome recurs or worsens with glucocorticoid tapering. Repeat bone marrow biopsy revealed 23% blasts, consistent with progression to acute myeloid leukemia. The patient opted for comfort measures and died 2 weeks later.

question: A healthy 27-year-old woman received a COVID-19 mRNA booster vaccine (Moderna) on December 7, 2021. She had not experienced adverse effects after the first 2 vaccine doses on January 17 and February 5, 2021. Twelve days after the booster vaccination, she developed pruritic wheals on her face and bilateral, transient eyelid swelling. Over the next week, a pruritic rash spread over her neck, chest, trunk, and arms; each lesion faded without scarring within 24 hours. She did not experience lip, tongue, or neck swelling; shortness of breath; wheezing; chest pain; or palpitations. Application of pressure to her forearm in a circular motion using a pen cap elicited wheal and flare lesions (Figure, left panel). On physical examination, performed 17 days after the onset of rash, her vital signs were normal. She had no tongue, lip, or throat swelling, and her lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. Wheal and flare lesions developed on her upper eyelids during the examination and resolved after approximately 30 minutes (Figure, right panel). Approximately 20% of people develop urticaria over their lifetime, with two-thirds experiencing acute urticaria, defined as lasting less than 6 weeks.6 Urticaria is considered chronic if it recurs over a duration of 6 weeks or longer.1Urticaria can occur spontaneously or may be induced by specific triggers. The most common type of inducible urticaria is dermatographism, meaning “to write on the skin.” Simple urticarial dermatographism, which is a benign condition that affects 1.5% to 5% of healthy individuals and is sometimes associated with atopic dermatitis,7 presents as nonpruritic wheals. Symptomatic dermatographism involves dermatographic skin wheals that are pruritic.Symptomatic dermatographism is initially treated with a nonsedating antihistamine, such as cetirizine or fexofenadine, which can be increased to up to 4 times standard dose if symptoms persist.1 Patients with persistent symptomatic dermatographism despite high-dose antihistamines may benefit from omalizumab or possibly leukotriene receptor antagonists.1While this patient’s symptomatic dermatographism could have occurred spontaneously, it may have been triggered by COVID-19 mRNA booster vaccination. Urticaria recurred in 3.3% and angioedema recurred in 2.6% of these individuals after their second COVID-19 mRNA vaccination.9 The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states that cutaneous reactions occurring more than 4 hours after COVID-19 vaccination are not a contraindication to subsequent vaccination.10The patient’s urticaria did not resolve with standard-dose fexofenadine (180 mg daily) or with 4 times the standard dose, so montelukast (10 mg nightly) and an additional midday dose of 360 mg fexofenadine was added. Twelve weeks after the onset of urticaria, she was given omalizumab (300 mg subcutaneously), montelukast was stopped, and fexofenadine was decreased to 360 mg twice daily. Two weeks after receiving omalizumab, her dermatographism resolved. Fexofenadine was decreased to 180 mg twice daily. The plan is to continue omalizumab monthly for a total of 3 doses. She was counseled to increase her dose of nonsedating antihistamines starting 3 days prior to another COVID-19 mRNA vaccination.

question: A 12-year-old girl with an unremarkable medical and ocular history was admitted for workup of anemia (hemoglobin, 6.7 g/dL; to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10) and leukopenia (white blood cell count, 1220 cells/μL; to convert to ×109 cells per liter, multiply by 0.001) with associated symptoms of headache, malaise, recent cough, and fever. Inflammatory markers were elevated with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate greater than 130 mm/h and a C-reactive protein level of 1.48 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10). The patient noted floaters in her right eye, which prompted an ophthalmology consultation. On bedside examination, her near visual acuity was J1+ (Snellen equivalent, 20/20 OU), and color vision was full in both eyes; the patient’s intraocular pressure, pupils, extraocular movements, and confrontational visual fields were all unremarkable. Dilated examination revealed grade I and II optic disc edema in the right and left eyes, respectively, and peripapillary hemorrhage in the right eye. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits with and without contrast and lumbar puncture were obtained, and results showed diffuse signal abnormality in the bone marrow compartment and findings suggestive of papilledema. Magnetic resonance venography did not reveal thrombosis. Opening pressure during lumbar puncture was 37 cm H2O (upper limit of normal, 28 cm H2O); all cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) viral serology test results were negative, and glucose level and red and white blood cell counts were all within normal limits. CSF protein was slightly decreased at 10.4 mg/dL, and CSF cytospin findings were unremarkable.Optical coherence tomography of the right (A) and left (B) optic discs showing edema (mean retinal nerve fiber layer thickness, 158 μm and 187 μm in the right and left eye, respectively). What Would You Do Next?
opb: Diagnose and treat idiopathic intracranial hypertension
explanation: The patient’s age, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, decreased white and red blood cell counts, signal abnormality within the bone marrow on MRI (Figure 2), and ocular findings raised suspicion for an oncologic process and precluded serial monitoring (choice A) and diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (choice B). Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myelocytic leukemia were considered as differential diagnoses, as were Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. question: A patient in their 60s with a medical history of hypertension was referred for new-onset fluctuating diplopia and worsening right upper eyelid ptosis. The patient underwent right-sided ptosis repair at another hospital less than 1 year earlier without improvement. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OU, and pupil examination revealed no anisocoria or afferent pupillary defect. Color vision was full in both eyes. External examination revealed a margin reflex distance 1 (MRD1) of 0 mm OD, 4 mm OS without fatigability in extended upgaze (Figure 1A). The patient had a small exotropia in primary gaze with a −2 supraduction deficit. No proptosis was observed. An ice pack was applied in the clinic to the ptotic eyelid for 2 minutes, which led to a 1.5-mm improvement (Figure 1B) in ptosis and no appreciable change in strabismus. The patient reported no associated headache, weakness, or difficulty swallowing.External photographs demonstrate ptosis of the right upper eyelid with a margin reflex distance 1 of 0 mm (A) that improved by 1.5 mm after application of an ice pack for 2 minutes (B).Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbit What Would You Do Next?
opb: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbit
opd: Begin symptomatic management with cholinesterase inhibitor
diagnosis: Superior divisional oculomotor nerve palsy due to internal carotid artery aneurysm
answer: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbit
explanation: The constellation of new-onset fluctuating diplopia and ptosis in a patient can suggest a diagnosis of ocular myasthenia gravis, especially in the setting of ptosis that improves with application of an ice pack. The ice test is a quick and effective examination that has been shown to be highly specific and sensitive in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.1-3 Although testing for antibodies (choice A) against the acetylcholine receptor or muscle-specific tyrosine kinase can help confirm a diagnosis of ocular myasthenia gravis, other etiologies must be ruled out, including orbital masses, cavernous sinus syndrome, and isolated oculomotor nerve palsy, some of which may be vision or life threatening.4,5Improvement of the ptotic eyelid is considered the hallmark of a positive ice test result, and initial studies evaluating the ice test revealed that patients with myasthenic ptosis typically demonstrate an improvement of 2 mm or greater in the MRD1.1,2 In contrast, patients with nonmyasthenic causes of ptosis, such as oculomotor nerve palsy and senile levator dehiscence, showed changes in the MRD1 (≤1 mm) that did not meet the threshold for a positive test result.1,2 Although an increase of 1.5 mm in the MRD1 as observed in this patient does not meet the criteria for a positive test result, it was greater than the typical changes observed in previously reported negative test results. Rare cases of false-positive test results have been observed in patients with chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia or cavernous sinus syndrome and after botulinum toxin injection.3,6 Although equivocal findings may lead to an eventual diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, other masquerading diagnoses should be considered prior to intervention (choice D) or repair (choice C).This patient presented with limitation in supraduction consistent with a superior divisional oculomotor palsy. To rule out etiologies with higher morbidity, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits was performed in addition to concomitant antibody testing. The magnetic resonance image revealed a 1.9-cm aneurysm in the right cavernous sinus leading to compression of the right internal carotid artery and oculomotor nerve, as well as a 5-mm aneurysm arising from the internal carotid artery in the left cavernous sinus (Figure 2). Compressive aneurysms along the cavernous, hypophyseal, and ophthalmic segments of the internal carotid artery are a well-described cause of oculomotor nerve palsy that may require neurosurgical or endovascular intervention. Variable diplopia due to aneurysmal causes has rarely been reported and is hypothesized to be due to intermittent hyperfunction of extraocular muscles innervated by the third cranial nerve.7 While rare, superior divisional palsies have been reported in cavernous carotid aneurysms, due to the bifurcation of the nerve at the anterior cavernous sinus into the superior and inferior division.8,9Axial T1-weighted magnetic resonance image of brain and orbits revealed a 1.9-cm aneurysm in the cavernous sinus (arrowhead), causing compression and medial deviation of the right internal carotid artery and subsequent compression of the oculomotor nerve. A small 5-mm aneurysm arising at the junction of the cavernous and supraclinoid segments of the left internal carotid artery was also noted but is not visualized on this image.This patient was diagnosed with oculomotor nerve palsy secondary to compressive aneurysm of the internal carotid artery in the right cavernous sinus and referred for neurosurgical intervention. The patient underwent embolization with improvement of the ptosis and diplopia.

question: A 65-year-old woman was referred with a 6-week history of blurry vision, ocular pain, and subconjunctival yellow discoloration in the left eye. Suspicious retinal detachment and intraocular mass were identified, which raised concerns for choroidal melanoma. No symptoms or signs were reported in the right eye. Her ocular history included bilateral cataract surgery 5 years prior. Review of systems yielded negative results, including for ocular trauma, jaundice, and cutaneous melanoma. She had no history of tobacco use.On examination of the left eye, visual acuity was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 8 mm Hg. The anterior segment showed diffuse conjunctival chemosis of yellow hue, low-grade aqueous reaction, and pseudophakia (Figure 1A). On the fundus evaluation, large pockets of subretinal fluid suggested choroidal effusion based on marked fluid shifting with head position. B-scan ultrasonography confirmed 4-quadrant choroidal hemorrhage and partially mobile serous retinal detachment. B-scans also exhibited a solid lesion from the 6- to 10-o’clock meridians with irregular shape and variable internal reflectivity, measuring 5.8 mm in height. Magnetic resonance imaging was requested to delineate the mass from the surrounding clot (Figure 1B). In the interim, she received oral steroids aiming to contain the abundant exudation and topical atropine for pain, evolving with minimal clinical improvement on these features.Coloration changes in the left eye associated with choroidal hemorrhage and an intraocular solid lesion. B, The arrowhead indicates the lesion and the asterisk, the adjacent clot. What Would You Do Next?
opa: Investigate liver dysfunction and biliary tract obstruction
opb: Drain the hemorrhage with scleral windows
opd: Rule out an occult systemic neoplasm
answer: Rule out an occult systemic neoplasm
explanation: Choroidal effusion consists of serous-hemorrhagic fluid accumulation in the suprachoroidal space typically encountered in trauma, surgery, or uveitis scenarios.1,2 It can produce a mass effect simulating tumors2 or be the presenting feature of ocular neoplasms,3 requiring elucidation as to its origin and nature. In this patient, disproportional choroidal exudation in the context of a solid lesion unresponsive to steroid therapy was strongly suggestive of malignancy.The yellow discoloration noted in only 1 eye was unusual and likely reflected a subacute process related to long-standing choroidal fluid buildup.4 Unlike the scleral impregnation with bilateral involvement classically seen in jaundice,5 the ocular coloration changes developed in this patient indicated a local mechanism, mediated by fluid extravasation from the choroidal compartment to the subconjunctival space.4 Therefore, screening for causes of bilirubin elevation, such as liver dysfunction and biliary tract obstruction (choice A), would not be the first step taken.Given the presence of an intraocular mass, primary and secondary neoplasms should be foremost investigated before any treatment consideration. Surgical drainage of the hemorrhagic content (choice B) and management with plaque brachytherapy (choice C) would not be advisable until a final diagnosis was reached because of risks of incomplete disease control and tumor seeding. Based on the characteristics of the lesion on imaging, notably heterogeneous reflectivity, irregular surface, and infiltrative pattern, which typically signal uveal metastasis as opposed to primary melanoma,6 screening for an occult systemic primary cancer should be the first course of action (choice D).Accordingly, the patient underwent full-body imaging studies with computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis. She was identified with a 6 × 9-cm silent mass at the upper left pulmonary lobe with associated mediastinal adenopathy (Figure 2). A fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the lung tumor revealed primary adenocarcinoma. Other metastatic lesions were also identified on the thoracic spine.Computed tomography scan reveals a lobular lung tumor (arrowhead).Metastasis is the most common ocular malignancy in the adult population, affecting the choroid in 85% of patients by hematogenous dissemination.6,7 Metastatic implants are visible on fundoscopy as single or multiple light-yellow solid lesions of variable shape usually with associated subretinal fluid.6 Primary sites have been localized, in order of frequency, to breast, lung, kidney, gastrointestinal tract, and cutaneous melanoma.7 In a large series, uveal metastasis from lung cancer was more prevalent in men (55%) and mainly unifocal (77%) and unilateral (82%).8 Approximately 40% of individuals had the original tumor discovered only after detecting uveal lesions8 similar to what we observed in this patient. Although choroidal effusion may be a nonspecific finding attributable to metastatic systemic neoplasms,3,6 a threshold of suspicion for underlying malignancy is advisable in the face of any intraocular solid growth.The patient was treated with systemic chemotherapy (entrectinib) and external beam radiotherapy to the mediastinum and orbits (20 Gy, 5 fractions). The conjunctival color progressively recovered in the following weeks, whereas the choroidal metastasis and detachment resolved 3 months after radiation. The visual acuity in the left eye remained hand motion.

question: An otherwise healthy man in his 20s presented to the dermatology department with thickening and swelling of hands after immersion in water, accompanied by burning pruritus for 3 years. The lesions occurred as symmetrical white and transparent papules, white keratosis, excessive wrinkling on the dorsum of hands after water immersion and worsened in summer, and remitted in winter. He was treated with topical tretinoin ointment intermittently per a diagnosis of chronic eczema at the local clinic with little improvement. The lesions gradually aggravated, and the affected area dispersed to wrists and elbows during past the 1.5 years. He attributed these changes to the need for washing hands frequently in the period of the COVID-19 epidemic. He had no family history of similar skin problems and did not have a history of hyperhidrosis, cystic fibrosis, atopy, or trauma to the hands.Physical examination showed some changes emerged on both hands after water immersion contrasting with any other condition (Figure, A and B). We took a skin biopsy specimen from white papules on the right hand, and representative histopathologic features are shown in the Figure, C and D.A and B, After immersing both hands in water for 10 mins, there were symmetrical white papules, white hyperkeratosis spots, and excessive wrinkling on the thenar eminence, wrist flexure of both hands, and dorsum of fingers and hands. C and D, A skin biopsy taken from white papules after water immersion for 10 mins showed hyperkeratosis, dilated eccrine ducts in the epidermis and dermis, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat glanda (hematoxylin-eosin). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed remarkable compact orthohyperkeratosis in the epidermis, dilatation of intraepidermal eccrine ducts, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat glands. However, the patient’s clinical process was quite interesting. The lesions only appeared after immersion in water, disappeared about 30 minutes after drying, and no lesions occurred with the absence of water contact. This unusual phenomenon, named “hand in the bucket sign,” showed that multiple white and transparent papules, excessive wrinkling on an erythema base with a clear linear border alongside the immersed area appeared on the thenar eminence, dorsum of fingers and hands, and wrists flexure of both hands after water contact for several minutes. The diagnosis can be confirmed as aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma based on contact history, clinical manifestation, and histopathologic change. The patient was treated with topical hydrocortisone urea ointment and recommended to avoid unnecessary contact with water. The symptoms had greatly improved after 1 month, and he is still in follow-up as of this writing.Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma (ASA) is a rare acquired skin disease that mostly occurs in female adolescents. Characteristic clinical manifestation is symmetrical, transparent-white papules and plagues. Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma is also known as the hand in the bucket sign because it appears transiently and recurrently eruptions after immersion into water, and resolves in minutes to hours after drying.1 The lesions are generally asymptomatic with occasional itching, stinging, burning, or even pain.Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma mostly affects the bilateral palms, sometimes also on soles, and rarely involves the dorsum of fingers2 and the medial heel according to previous reports.3 In this case, the patient manifested unusual involvements of the dorsal areas of hands, wrists, elbows, with the palm areas spared, which, to our knowledge has previously not been reported.It is easy to misdiagnose ASA as eczema when the clinical features first appear without characteristic involvement. Furthermore, ASA is distinguished with progressive symmetric erythrokeratoderma that presents well-demarcated erythematous and keratotic plaques covered with thin scales initially on the bilateral palms, while not aggravating after water immersion. Another crucial differential diagnosis is hereditary papulotranslucent acrokeratoderma, which appears after puberty and persists for a lifetime. The clinical manifestation is persistent asymptomatic lesions, associated with fine-textured scalp hair and an atopic diathesis, whereas it presents pathologic findings of focal hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, and normal eccrine ducts.4 The diagnosis of ASA is mostly based on the contact history and clinical manifestations. question: On the day of giving birth via a normal vaginal delivery, a healthy woman in her 20s developed painful swelling on her right thigh, at the site of a methergine injection administered 1 day prior. Despite 3 days of treatment with an oral antibiotic (cefalexin), her thigh pain and swelling did not improve, and she was readmitted to the hospital and intravenous clindamycin was started. Wound cultures and blood cultures obtained during incision and drainage performed on hospital day 1 were negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal organisms. The following day, her temperature was 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), blood pressure was 86/42 mm Hg, and heart rate was 131/min. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for presumed septic shock, and her antibiotics were changed to vancomycin and meropenem. Surgical debridement of the right thigh was performed on hospital day 3.On hospital day 4, a new purple dusky border developed along the wound edge, and the patent underwent a second surgical debridement. After debridement on hospital day 5, her temperature was 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), and she required vasopressor infusion with norepinephrine for shock. Her right thigh had a deep 9 × 8–cm ulcer with a dusky violaceous border extending 2 to 5 cm from the wound edge (Figure, left), with many 1- to 2-mm pustules (not visible in Figure). Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 30 000/μL (88% neutrophils); lactate level, 77.5 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L); and procalcitonin level, 16.1 ng/mL (reference, <0.1 ng/mL). Histologic examination of the tissue obtained during the second surgical debridement revealed ulceration with extensive neutrophilic inflammation (Figure, right). Stains for microorganisms, and tissue and blood cultures, remained negative.Left, Patient’s right thigh showing characteristic violaceous border surrounding the surgical wound edge after multiple debridements. explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis of necrotizing pyoderma gangrenosum in this case was the presence of a dusky ulcer with a violaceous border, histopathologic findings of a dense pan-dermal neutrophilic infiltrate (Figure, right), and absence of an infectious organism on multiple blood and tissue cultures. Because pyoderma gangrenosum is an inflammatory condition, additional antifungal therapy (choice A) is not effective, and additional surgical debridement (choice B) could worsen the condition because of pathergy. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (choice C) may be used for wound healing but would not resolve the inflammation associated with pyoderma gangrenosum.Neutrophilic dermatoses are a heterogenous group of inflammatory, noninfectious skin disorders that present with a sterile, neutrophilic infiltrate on histopathology.1,2 Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare inflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis with an estimated worldwide incidence of 3 to 10 cases per million people per year, with a female to male ratio of 1.8:1 across all ages.3 Pyoderma gangrenosum typically presents with ulcerative (classic), bullous, pustular, or vegetative lesions. Early lesions of ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum appear as tender erythematous nodules or papulopustules that can erode to create ulcers with a purulent base and inflammatory, violaceous, and overhanging borders. More than half of patients develop pyoderma gangrenosum in association with an underlying systemic disease, such as inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or hematologic malignancy. Pyoderma gangrenosum is also associated with pathergy, a condition in which trauma to the skin (such as surgical debridement) results in skin lesions or ulcers that may be resistant to healing.4-6 In this patient, the methergine injection likely served as the source of pathergy.Pyoderma gangrenosum and Sweet syndrome, a neutrophilic dermatosis typically characterized by painful nodules or plaques, may present with systemic symptoms that can mimic necrotizing fasciitis or severe infection, including fever, shock, and leukocytosis.4,7 Necrotizing neutrophilic dermatosis has been recently proposed as a unifying term for necrotizing pyoderma gangrenosum and necrotizing Sweet syndrome4 and is characterized by histopathologic findings of diffuse dermal and subcutaneous neutrophilic infiltration with necrosis, negative blood and tissue cultures, and prominent clinical signs or symptoms of systemic inflammation (such as leukocytosis and shock).1Pyoderma gangrenosum is frequently misdiagnosed, which can lead to a delay in appropriate treatment as well as unnecessary and ineffective treatment with antibiotics. Moreover, surgical debridement may worsen pyoderma gangrenosum through pathergy. Key diagnostic criteria for pyoderma gangrenosum recently proposed by international expert panels include development of a progressive ulcer with a neutrophilic infiltrate seen on histologic examination, no evidence of an infectious cause (negative tissue culture and special stains for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria), and a therapeutic response to immunosuppressants.8,9 In addition, workup for hematologic malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, and rheumatoid arthritis should be performed for individuals diagnosed with pyoderma gangrenosum.First-line treatment of pyoderma gangrenosum involves use of systemic glucocorticoids over the course of days to weeks.1,2,4 Glucocorticoid-sparing treatments, including infliximab and cyclosporine, can also be used.1,10On hospital day 6, intravenous methylprednisolone (25 mg every 8 hours) was started; within 24 hours, the patient’s vital signs normalized and vasopressors were discontinued. Glucocorticoids were stopped after 3 days, and she remained in the hospital for wound care until postoperative day 14, when she was discharged home with a vacuum-assisted closure of her wound. The wound closure device was removed 8 weeks later, at which point her wound had healed. The patient has not had a recurrence of pyoderma gangrenosum in more than 3 years.

explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of subacute joint pain along with a saddle nose deformity, which was revealed when the patient removed her face mask. The differential diagnosis of saddle nose deformity includes relapsing polychondritis, sarcoidosis, granulomatous infections (such as syphilis and leprosy), neoplasms, intranasal drug use, and trauma. However, the combination of saddle nose deformity, arthralgias, and acute kidney injury with red blood cell casts and proteinuria is highly suggestive of systemic small-vessel vasculitis such as GPA.Although lupus nephritis and scleroderma renal crisis may cause hematuria, proteinuria, and worsening kidney function, these diseases are not associated with saddle nose deformity, so checking antinuclear antibodies and complement levels (choice B) is less useful. Conventional angiography of the aorta and renal arteries (choice C) can identify renal artery aneurysms and stenoses. However, a medium-vessel vasculitis affecting the renal arteries, such as polyarteritis nodosa, does not typically present with glomerulonephritis. While checking RPR and a fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (choice D) is reasonable to work up causes of saddle nose deformity, syphilis does not typically cause glomerulonephritis.GPA, formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis, is a potentially life-threatening small-vessel vasculitis characterized by the presence of ANCA targeting neutrophil-specific granule proteins. GPA causes necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in small blood vessels throughout the body, most commonly affecting the capillary beds of the kidneys, lungs, and skin. GPA affects men and women equally and is rare, with an incidence of 0.4 to 11.9 cases per million person-years and prevalence of 2.3 to 146.0 cases per million persons.1GPA may cause inflammation of the upper respiratory tract, resulting in crusting rhinitis, otitis, subglottic stenosis, and sinusitis. Chronic granulomatous sinusitis due to GPA can lead to bone and cartilage destruction, resulting in collapse of the nasal bridge, which causes the appearance of a saddle nose deformity. GPA also commonly affects the lower respiratory tract (lung granuloma, alveolar hemorrhage), kidney (pauci-immune glomerulonephritis), and skin (palpable purpura). Systemic symptoms such as arthralgias, fever, and fatigue are frequently experienced by patients with GPA. Kidney involvement, often in the form of RPGN, occurs in up to 70% of patients with GPA. Early diagnosis of GPA is important to avoid progression to kidney failure, which occurs in approximately one quarter of patients with RPGN.2Patients with GPA most commonly have a cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) pattern and antibodies directed against proteinase 3 (PR3), which is located in neutrophils and monocytes. However, a smaller proportion of patients demonstrate a perinuclear staining pattern (p-ANCA) with antibodies typically directed against myeloperoxidase (MPO).1 Although kidney biopsy is not required to diagnose GPA, it is helpful to confirm the diagnosis of GPA in the setting of pulmonary-renal syndrome (to exclude anti–glomerular basement membrane disease) or in patients with suspected GPA but negative ANCA and absence of antibodies directed against MPO or PR3.Induction therapy for patients with organ-threatening complications of GPA includes rituximab and high-dose glucocorticoids.3 Cyclophosphamide can also be used for induction of remission,4 but it may be associated with greater toxicity than rituximab.5-7 For maintenance of remission, the most commonly used medications are rituximab, methotrexate, or azathioprine.8Blood testing in this patient revealed p-ANCA at 1:160 dilution and presence of anti-MPO antibodies. Kidney biopsy demonstrated a pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis, confirming the diagnosis of GPA. She was initially treated with rituximab and prednisone, 1 mg/kg/d. Prednisone was tapered over the next 6 months to her current dose of 5 mg/d, with resolution of her joint pain. At 15 months from induction of remission, she continues to receive rituximab as maintenance therapy and her kidney function has recovered to baseline. Her nasal deformity was successfully treated with reconstructive surgery.

He reported diplopia and pain with extraocular movement. There were no constitutional, dermatologic, or neurologic symptoms. Visual acuity and neurologic and fundus examination findings were otherwise normal with no sign of optic neuropathy.Patient characteristics at initial presentation. explanation: The patient had features of a corticosteroid-responsive bilateral orbital myositis (OM). OM was first described in 1903.1  It can occur at any age and more commonly affects women.2  It commonly presents as painful diplopia or orbital inflammation with chemosis, proptosis, or conjunctival hyperemia. The horizontal recti muscles are most frequently affected, although the superior or inferior recti can also be involved.3  The inflammatory process (Figure 2) appears to be mediated by helper T-cell type 1, with significant elevations in interleukin 12, tumor necrosis factor α, and interferon γ.4 Diagnosis of OM is based on physical examination and radiologic features excluding other etiologies and may require tissue biopsy when features are atypical or response to corticosteroids is inadequate.Left lateral rectus muscle biopsy results show prominent chronic inflammatory infiltrates composed of a mixture of epithelioid histiocytes and small-sized lymphocytes, associated with markedly atrophic residual skeletal muscle fibers (yellow arrowheads) and scattered eosinophils (blue arrowheads) (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×200).Acute idiopathic OM is the most common form of OM and typically affects a single muscle and is corticosteroid responsive. Recurrent OM occurs in 15% of patients and is more common in men. OM is more likely to be recurrent if multiple extraocular muscles are involved on presentation or if there is a lack of response to initial corticosteroid treatment.2,5 In such cases, adverse effects from long-term corticosteroids often necessitate the use of alternative maintenance therapy, such as infliximab, rather than continuing corticosteroids indefinitely (option A).6Autoimmune and infectious causes of OM should be considered in atypical cases and include IgG4-related disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, spondyloarthropathies, vasculitis, Lyme disease, herpes zoster, and cysticercosis. Ocular manifestations occur in 3% of patients with IBD,7 although IBD-associated OM is a rare extraintestinal manifestation, which is more commonly bilateral and recurrent.8Medication-induced OM has been reported, particularly with bisphosphonates and monoclonal antibody therapies, and usually occurs early after commencing treatment. question: A 49-year-old African American woman with no significant medical history came to the clinic because of abnormal retinal findings and mildly decreased visual acuity. She was told about these same findings 10 years ago but did not have a repeated eye examination until recently by another retina specialist. She reported no family history of retinal diseases. She initially received anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) treatment, but was later referred because of a concern about either the idiopathic or paraneoplastic variant of acute exudative polymorphous vitelliform maculopathy (AEPVM). Initial workup by her primary care physician was unremarkable for malignancy. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/60 OD and 20/50 OS. An anterior segment examination was normal. Dilated fundus examination revealed multiple vitelliform lesions involving the macula and superior macula bilaterally (Figure 1). Fluorescein angiography revealed staining of these lesions with a pseudohypopyon appearance of the central vitelliform lesion in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed hyperreflectance corresponding to the yellow pigment in the vitelliform lesions in the subretinal space. No evidence of a choroidal neovascular membrane was present on examination or imaging.Computed tomographic scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis What Would You Do Next?
opa: Computed tomographic scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis
explanation: This patient had multifocal Best disease, a variant of Best disease. Best disease is typically an autosomal dominant maculopathy caused by mutations in the BEST1 (VMD2) gene, resulting in abnormal lipofuscin accumulation in the macula. These patients typically show symptoms in the first 2 decades of life with a classic “egg yolk” lesion in the central macula. Further retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) thinning and pigment changes arise as this lesion breaks down in the “pseudohypopyon stage,” with corresponding hyperautofluorescence of this pseudohypopyon demonstrated on fundus autofluorescence1 ,2 (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography demonstrates hyperreflectance corresponding to the lipofuscin in the subretinal space. Eventually all of the yellow pigment may be taken up, leaving behind corresponding atrophic retinal pigment epithelium. Patients typically maintain good BCVA, often 20/30 to 20/40, unless a choroidal neovascular membrane develops. Electroretinography is typically normal, but the electro-oculogram is abnormal with a low ratio of light peak to dark trough (Arden ratio).Fundus autofluorescence of the left eye, with optical coherence tomography of the left eye (inset).A less commonly described variation of the disease is known as autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy, related to an autosomal recessive mutation of the BEST1 gene on chromosome 11. Examination often reveals diffuse retinal pigment epithelium changes with multifocal whitish or yellowish punctate deposits seen in the macula and mid periphery.3 In this patient, the vitelliform lesions were multifocal within the macula, though larger than the lesions seen in autosomal recessive bestrophinopathy. Genetic testing revealed that she was heterozygous for a BEST1 gene mutation, suggesting an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.Differentiating Best disease from idiopathic and paraneoplastic AEPVM is challenging because of significant overlap on examination and imaging. Idiopathic AEPVM presents bilaterally as serous retinal detachments with vitelliform deposits or bleblike lesions along the arcades; these lesions can regress in the span of months. Patients with paraneoplastic AEPVM may have a history of cancer, especially melanoma or BRAF/MEK inhibitor usage, and may present unilaterally.4,5 To date, no patient with AEPVM has shown mutations in BEST1 or peripherin/RDS, making genetic testing a highly useful diagnostic tool given the clinical similarities.6Lesions do not respond to anti-VEGF therapy if no choroidal neovascular membrane is present (choice B). Given the patient’s 10-year history of these ocular lesions without systemic issues, as well as her initial negative workup, whole-body imaging (choice A) and antiretinal antibody testing (choice D) may not need to be the next immediate steps in workup. However, in the absence of an established diagnosis and negative genetic results, whole-body imaging should be pursued to rule out malignancy.Recently, genetic testing via saliva testing has become a reliable and accessible resource that may be more cost-effective and convenient than electrophysiologic testing.7 As more gene therapies become available for patients, genetic testing will have a greater influence on management and prognosis.8 In this case, genetic testing provided a definitive diagnosis that helped rule out a potentially life-threatening diagnosis.The patient was reassured that her condition was not paraneoplastic nor immediately blinding. Whole-body imaging was performed at a later time for unrelated medical issues, and no occult malignancy was found. She is being evaluated semiannually with ancillary OCT and fundus autofluorescence.

question: A White woman in her 40s was referred to an outside ophthalmologist after developing nausea and a headache following a dilated eye examination. She was found to have narrow angles in both eyes and a laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) was performed in her left eye. Two weeks later she developed flickering photopsias and a temporal scotoma progressing to a “brown tint” of her vision in her left eye. Her vision had decreased in her left eye and macular and optic nerve edema were noted and she was subsequently referred to us. In our clinic, her visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/50 OS, and she had normal intraocular pressure, a shallow anterior chamber but open angle in both eyes, a patent LPI in the left eye, and clear crystalline lenses in both eyes. The rest of her anterior segment was unremarkable. The posterior examination was notable for shifting subretinal fluid with choroidal detachments without retinal breaks, inflammation, or optic nerve edema and leopard spotting, while her right eye was unremarkable (Figure, A). Fluorescein angiography was unrevealing, while optical coherence tomography showed shallow subretinal fluid and an irregular and thickened choroid (Figure, B). Ultrasonography showed an axial length of 20.0 mm, thickened sclera, anteriorly rotated ciliary body, and 360° of ciliochoroidal detachments in both eyes but worse in the left eye. Results of a systemic laboratory evaluation for infectious and noninfectious disorders were unremarkable. Systemic corticosteroids failed to resolve the subretinal fluid and her vision declined.Subretinal fluid and choroidal effusions following a laser peripheral iridotomy. A, Fundus photography showed substantial choroidal effusions with overlying serous retinal detachments (asterisk). B, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging identified choroidal congestion, thickening, and undulations as well as shallow subretinal fluid.Perform a clear lens exchange in the left eye What Would You Do Next?
opa: Repeat LPI in the left eye
opb: Perform an LPI in the right eye
opd: Perform a clear lens exchange in the left eye
explanation: Despite high-dose corticosteroids, vision continued to decline and the choroidal effusions and retinal detachment enlarged in the left eye making a subtle, underlying inflammatory-driven disorder unlikely. With small effusions and shallow anterior chamber in the right eye as well, her presentation was unlikely related to the LPI alone. Prolonged hypotony, malignant hypertension, underlying causes of elevated uveal venous pressure (eg, pulmonary hypertension, arteriovenous fistulas, and Sturge-Weber syndrome), uveal effusion syndrome, and several neoplastic conditions are other underlying etiologies of choroidal effusions. However, this patient’s blood pressure had been within normal limits at multiple measurements, she had no known underlying systemic diseases with an unremarkable echocardiogram and pulmonary function test results, and a thorough review of systems did not raise concern for cancer. Thus, this patient’s presentation was most consistent with idiopathic uveal effusion syndrome. On follow-up, the patient’s intraocular pressure had remained within normal ranges making a repeated LPI in the left eye incorrect as she had not developed angle closure (choice A). Furthermore, her current condition had likely been exacerbated by the original LPI. The response in the left eye also would make choice B potentially dangerous because of concern of instigating a similar set of events in the right eye and not solve the worsening issues within the left eye. While a clear lens exchange (choice D) is an effective solution to narrow angles and a shallow anterior chamber, surgical complications are common in eyes with abnormal sclera.1,2 Further, choice D would only address a by-product of the underlying process, narrow angles, and not the disease itself but incur substantial surgical risk making it incorrect.3 While a recent randomized trial showed that cataract surgery with concurrent sclerostomy reduced perioperative complications in nanophthalmic eyes including the development of choroidal effusions, the surgeries were performed in eyes that did not already have choroidal effusions.3 There are 3 subtypes of uveal effusion syndrome.4 Nanophthalmic eyes with hyperopia (type I) and eyes with histologically abnormal sclera but otherwise normal (type II) respond to sclerectomies; however, otherwise normal eyes (type III) do not respond to sclerectomy.4,5 This patient with type II idiopathic uveal effusion syndrome needed the underlying pathophysiology addressed, her abnormal and thick sclera, with a 4-quadrant nearly full-thickness sclerectomy (choice C).6 The choroidal effusions and serous detachment improved following the procedure but did not fully resolve. Thus, a second 4-quadrant sclerectomy with 2 full-thickness sclerostomies were performed resulting in complete resolution of the choroidal effusions and continued improvement in the serous retinal detachment.This case shows idiopathic uveal effusion syndrome that appears to have been exacerbated by an LPI. Several groups have reported choroidal effusions developing after an LPI and other ocular laser procedures; however, in none of these cases did the patient develop concurrent serous detachments.7,8 In a large case series on uveal effusion syndrome and sclerectomies, a single procedure resulted in 83% of eyes with an anatomical success and increased to 96% after a second procedure.5 This resulted in visual improvement by 2 or more lines in 56% of eyes, stabilization in 35%, and worsening in only 9%.5 Prophylactic sclerectomies should be considered in nanophthalmic eyes or eyes with abnormally thick sclera when ocular surgery is being planned to reduce the risk of developing uveal effusions and serous detachments and the associated vision loss.9After two 4-quadrant nearly full-thickness sclerectomies, the patient’s choroidal effusions resolved and her serous retinal detachment nearly resolved. Her visual acuity was 20/40 OS at postoperative month 1. In the future, prophylactic sclerectomies in the right eye will be performed once the left eye has stabilized because of continued shallowing of her anterior chamber.

question: A white man in his early 80s with history of autoimmune pancreatitis, recurrent colon polyps, and benign prostatic hyperplasia developed rapid, painless vision loss of both eyes over a 2-week period 6 months after cataract surgery. Vision was 20/250 OD and 20/60 OS. The anterior segment was unremarkable in either eye, while the posterior segment examination noted 1+ vitreous cell, asteroid hyalosis, and a multilobulated, serous retinal detachment (RD) in the right eye and trace vitreous cell and a multilobulated, serous RD in the left eye. Imaging included B-scan, optical coherence tomography, and fundus autofluorescence, which revealed diffuse choroidal and ciliary body thickening, multifocal pockets of subretinal fluid, and speckled hyperautofluorescence and hypoautofluorescence in both eyes (Figure 1). No poliosis or skin changes were noted. A review of systems was unremarkable, most notably a lack of any pulmonary symptoms. A focused laboratory evaluation identified a significantly elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level and antinuclear antibody titer, but serum lysozyme, syphilis, and tuberculosis testing had negative results. To better differentiate between Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome, a lymphoproliferative disorder, or sarcoidosis as the underlying cause of the vitreous inflammation and multilobulated, serous RD in both eyes, a computed tomographic scan was performed. It showed marked lymphadenopathy throughout the mediastinum and diffuse scleral thickening in both eyes. The institute’s radiologists believed these computed tomography findings were nonspecific and could be indicative of either sarcoidosis or intraocular lymphoma.Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome–like presentation of multilobulated pockets of subretinal fluid and choroidal thickening and undulations. opb: Inject intravitreal antibiotics for endophthalmitis in both eyes

opd: Treat the patient with systemic steroids for presumed VKH syndrome
diagnosis: Biopsy-proven, Harada-like ocular sarcoidosis in both eyes

explanation: With the patient’s advanced age and inconclusive clinical picture, the diagnosis of a lymphoproliferative disorder vs sarcoidosis was unclear, and a biopsy was considered necessary for definitive diagnosis. With primarily choroidal and ciliary body involvement in both eyes, the sensitivity of a diagnostic vitrectomy for intraocular lymphoma was believed to be insufficient because of the relatively mild vitritis (choice A). Although some advocate a combined pars plana vitrectomy with choroidal biopsy in cases such as this one to increase diagnostic yields, we wanted to avoid, if possible, complications related to operating on an eye with active uveitis (eg, hypotony, inducing rhegmatogenous RD).1 The protracted course, unremarkable review of systems, and lack of pain or hypopyon made an underlying infectious etiology unlikely (choice B). Because of the diagnostic dilemma, conflicting treatment algorithms, and risk of future central nervous system involvement with intraocular lymphoma, an incisional flap-based ciliary body–choroidal biopsy was performed in the right eye (choice C). An initial approach with ocular biopsy was favored because of the difficult location of many of the enlarged lymph nodes within the patient’s chest. Systemic corticosteroids were not given until the biopsy could be performed because of the concern that their use may limit diagnostic yield (choice D).2Pathological changes within the choroid were consistent with sarcoidosis with multiple, multinucleated giant cells and noncaseating granulomas (Figure 2). Because of the enlarged lymph nodes and concern about an additional process, our colleagues performed a biopsy of the lymph nodes; those results were also consistent with sarcoidosis. Staining the ciliary body biopsy sample revealed multiple giant cells, enlarged in inset (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×10 and inset ×40).This case highlights the importance of a tissue diagnosis in uveitis, especially when the treatment algorithms and prognosis could vary (eg, local and systemic chemotherapeutics for lymphoma vs corticosteroids and immunomodulatory therapy for sarcoidosis).4 Furthermore, this patient’s presentation was unusual: an isolated, sarcoid-associated, posterior uveitis is uncommon, reported in only 12% of all cases of ocular sarcoidosis, and only 6% of serous RDs in patients with uveitis can be attributed to sarcoidosis.5,6 However, an isolated posterior uveitis associated with sarcoidosis represents the largest portion of patients with severe vision loss attributed to the disease and is a documented risk factor for poor visual outcomes.5,7 To complicate matters, VKH syndrome and sarcoidosis may have a similar underlying genetic risk factor, and patients can develop both sequentially.8,9 Although multilobulated, serous RDs with intraocular inflammation are most commonly associated with VKH syndrome, intraocular lymphoma and sarcoidosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis.The patient’s systemic corticosteroids were tapered and oral methotrexate continued. He is currently being monitored every 6 months.

question: A patient in their 50s presented with asymptomatic keratotic papules, first noticed on the left middle and ring fingers and left toe web spaces more than 10 years earlier. The papules progressed proximally over the subsequent decade to involve the forearm, arm, scapular area, ankle, shin, and thigh, but only affected the left side of the body. The patient’s face, palms, soles, and entire right side of the body were spared. The patient has a history of rosacea being treated with topical metronidazole gel for flares but was otherwise asymptomatic. The patient did not have any alopecia, night blindness, or dry eyes or skin. There was no history of any exposure to radiation or arsenic, nutritional deficiency, inflammatory skin disease, or malignant neoplasm. There was no family history of a similar condition.Examination revealed multiple, submillimeter, skin-colored to yellowish keratotic spiny projections over the aforementioned areas, only on the left side of the body (Figure, A and B). Punch biopsy from a lesion showed orthokeratosis with parakeratotic columns emerging from an epidermal invagination. The epidermis was mildly acanthotic and with a normal granular layer. There was a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Adjacent hair follicles were unaffected (Figure, C).A, Numerous, submillimeter, skin-colored spiny projections over left foot web spaces were present. B, Close-up photograph over the left scapular area showed lesions of similar morphologic characteristics. C, Histologic results showed a parakeratotic column overlying a mildly acanthotic epidermis with a normal granular layer and keratinocyte maturation. A sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate was present (hematoxylin-eosin). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis (MMDH) is a rare disorder of keratinization, first coined by Goldstein in 1967.1 To our knowledge, only 27 female and 11 male cases of MMDH have been reported worldwide, with age at onset ranging from 4 months to 83 years, including this case.2,3 Several synonymous terms for MMDH exist in the medical literature (eg, familial disseminated piliform hyperkeratosis, disseminated spiked hyperkeratosis, minute aggregate keratosis).4Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis is characterized by multiple submillimeter spiky projections or spicules, usually located on the trunk and limbs in a symmetrical nonfollicular distribution, classically sparing the face and palmoplantar surfaces.4 They are often asymptomatic. The lesions can also be dome-shaped, flat-topped, or crateriform papules. White, yellowish, brown, or skin-colored variants have been described too.Typical histological features include focal columns of orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis arising from a tented epidermis, but there are cases of parakeratosis and epidermal invagination. The stratum granulosum is usually prominent but may be of variable thickness. Electron microscopy shows focally reduced number of keratohyalin granules and normal to increased number of lamellar (Odland) bodies.5The pathogenesis of MMDH remains unknown. It can be sporadic, familial (autosomal dominant trait inheritance), or drug induced (cyclosporine, etretinate, simvastatin, antifungal).6,7 A postinflammatory form associated with radiotherapy and solar irradiation has also been described. It is a nonfollicular digitate keratosis, whereas lichen spinulosus is a follicular digitate keratosis affecting the trunk and limbs. Lichen spinulosus occurs mostly in children and adolescents, where it presents as plaques of follicular spines. Porokeratosis lesions have characteristic ridges on the border (cornoid lamella) and a central furrow. Histologic findings show parakeratotic columns overlying a vertical zone of dyskeratotic and vacuolated cells within the epidermis. Viral warts present as solitary or multiple verrucous papules, usually larger than the submillimeter lesions seen in MMDH. Histologic findings also demonstrate a hypergranulomatosis papillomatous epidermis with overlying tiers of parakeratosis.Other differential diagnoses should be excluded too. Spiny keratoderma presents with discrete keratotic plugs on the palms, soles, or both. The predilection of acral sites in spiny keratoderma is typically not seen in MMDH. question: A teenaged boy presented to the outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of asymptomatic cutaneous lesions on the face that had progressively spread to the trunk and extremities. He also had asthenia and mild intermittent arthralgias. Physical examination revealed multiple millimetric erythematous to hyperpigmented monomorphic keratotic papules involving the head, trunk, and extremities. Symmetric annular brown erythematous plaques on the cheeks and temples were also seen. There were no vesicles or pustules (Figure, A and B). Laboratory investigations revealed a normal white blood cell count, mild anemia (hemoglobin level, 11.3 g/dL; normal level 12.50-15.50 g/dL; to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), hypocomplementemia, and moderate proteinuria. Autoimmune serology results showed raised levels of antinuclear antibodies (>1:160), anti-Smith antibodies, SSA/Ro antibodies, SSB/La antibodies, and anti-U1RNP antibodies. Anti-dsDNA antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, rheumatoid factor, IgG and IgM anticardiolipin antibody, and anti-β2 glycoprotein 1 antibody results were negative. A biopsy specimen obtained from an erythematous papule on the trunk and stained with hematoxylin-eosin is shown in the Figure, C and D.A, Millimetric erythematous to hyperpigmented monomorphic papules involving the trunk. B, Erythematous papules and symmetric annular brown erythematous plaques on the cheeks and temples. C and D, Punch biopsy results (hematoxylin-eosin). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Histopathological examination revealed a slightly atrophic epidermis with interface dermatitis, individual dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils, admixed with numerous mononuclear histiocytoid cells. Few eosinophils and leukocytoclastic debris were apparent, but there was no evidence of subepidermal blister formation or vasculitis. Immunohistochemical study results revealed that the mononuclear histiocytoid cells showed immunoreactivity for myeloperoxidase and CD68, suggesting myeloid lineage. Direct immunofluorescence showed negative results.The presence of a prominent infiltrate of neutrophils with leukocytoclasia, as well as an interface dermatitis, supported the diagnosis of nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus (NBNLE) in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).1 The patient was treated with oral prednisone and hydroxychloroquine with partial resolution of the lesions.Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus,2,3 also known as SLE-associated neutrophilic dermatosis3 or Sweet-like neutrophilic dermatosis,4 is a newly recognized clinicopathological variant of cutaneous lupus erythematosus characterized by the presence of a dermal and/or subcutaneous infiltrate of neutrophils and variable degrees of interface dermatitis.2,3,5 The disease predominantly affects women and is clinically manifested by multiple, usually nonpruritic, urticarial papules and nodules occurring in a wide distribution.2,3 Lesions most commonly develop in patients with SLE, especially in those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. However, they can also be the presenting manifestation of the disease.3 Histologically, NBNLE is characterized by a perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils with prominent leukocytoclasia and variable degrees of vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction. The neutrophilic infiltrate is usually superficial but can extend into the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.3,6 There is no evidence of vasculitis, necrobiosis, or prominent dermal edema, and direct immunofluorescence study results show complement and/or immunoglobulin deposition along the basement membrane zone in about half of cases. Exceptionally, a dermal infiltrate primarily composed of histiocyte-like immature myeloid cells has also been described.7,8 The differential diagnosis of NBNLE includes other conditions associated with SLE, such as acute lupus erythematosus, Sweet syndrome, hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis, and palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis. In the rare cases of NBNLE with histiocyte-like immature myeloid cells, histiocytoid Sweet syndrome can be considered. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus can be distinguished from acute lupus erythematosus by its more persistent and widespread distribution of cutaneous lesions and more pronounced dermal neutrophilic infiltrate.Sweet and histiocytoid Sweet syndrome lack vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction and show a denser infiltrate of neutrophils with prominent papillary dermal edema. Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis show cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis, and palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis show variable degrees of degenerated collagen and palisaded histiocytes.The pathogenesis of NBNLE is still unknown and seems to be complex. The combination of interface dermatitis and neutrophilic infiltrates suggests that both the innate and adaptive immune system may be involved. The prognosis of NBNLE is usually good but depends on the severity of the associated SLE. Lesions usually respond promptly to systemic corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, or dapsone.9,10 In case of persistence, mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine have also been used with good response.2,3 The present case highlights the wide range of clinicopathological features of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Increased awareness of this peculiar variant is important, as it may be the first clinical manifestation of SLE.

question: A patient with a history of normal-tension glaucoma presented with a blurred spot in the central vision of the right eye. Examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/50 OD, 20/30 OS, and intraocular pressure of 13 mm Hg OU. In the right eye, dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula revealed subretinal fluid and cystoid spaces within the outer nuclear layer and inner nuclear layer in the nasal macula (Figure 1). Results of the left eye fundus examination and macular OCT were normal. In both eyes, the optic cup appeared very deep with a large cup-disc ratio.Color fundus photograph (A) and optical coherence tomography of the macula (B) illustrating intraretinal and subretinal fluid at the nasal macula. The white line indicates the position of the optical coherence tomography scan.Five years prior to presentation, the patient started treatment with latanoprost nightly in both eyes for an enlarged cup-disc ratio presumed due to normal-tension glaucoma. At that time, intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS and central corneal thickness was normal. Visual field and OCT of the retinal nerve fiber layer were without reproducible defects over 5 years of follow-up. The patient denied a family history of eye disease. What Would You Do Next?
opc: OCT of the optic nerve head
answer: OCT of the optic nerve head
explanation: The differential diagnosis of macular fluid includes choroidal neovascularization, central serous chorioretinopathy, myopic foveoschisis, optic pit maculopathy, and cystoid macular edema. In this case, the subretinal and intraretinal fluid in multiple retinal layers contiguous with the optic nerve point to the optic nerve, rather than vascular leakage, as the source of the fluid. Therefore, fluorescein angiography (choice B) and OCT-angiography of the macula (choice D), tests that detect vascular sources of fluid, are not indicated, and anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (choice A), a treatment for vascular leakage, is not appropriate.Although optic pit maculopathy without inner retinal schisis cavity has been reported, the pattern and distribution of fluid is most consistent with optic pit maculopathy.1 ,2 However, clinical examination and OCT of the optic nerve revealed a very deep cup (1388 μm from the Bruch membrane opening) without a focal depression seen in optic pit (Figure 2).Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve head illustrating a very deep cup without a focal optic pit.Glaucoma can lead to increased cup depth, although this patient's cup depth is far outside the range seen in glaucoma.3 Excessively deep optic cups have been reported in optic pit but are common in cavitary optic disc anomaly (CODA).4 Rarely, macular schisis occurs secondary to glaucoma,5 but the normal intraocular pressure, normal retinal nerve fiber layer on OCT, very deep optic cup, and normal visual fields (data not shown) make CODA, rather than glaucoma, the likely diagnosis in this patient.Congenital excavated optic nerve abnormalities (optic nerve coloboma, optic pit, morning glory anomaly, and CODA) have a risk of vision loss around age 20 to 40 years due to macular fluid.4 These abnormalities are usually unilateral and sporadic, but are rarely autosomal dominant because of a triplication upstream of the MMP19 gene,6,7 which encodes an extracellular matrix protease in the optic nerve.6 In CODA, optic nerve abnormalities are highly penetrant with variable phenotype (optic pit, morning glory, atypical coloboma, glaucomatous cupping, and excessively deep optic cups).4 The central retinal artery is often not visible and retinal vessels appear to emanate directly from the cup edge. The optic cup may gradually enlarge, and excavation may develop from a previously normal optic nerve.7 These features of CODA mimic glaucoma, but should not be confused to avoid unnecessary treatments.In excavated optic nerve abnormalities, histologic studies and swept-source OCT imaging reveal that dysplastic retina herniates through the lamina cribrosa or juxtapapillary sclera and protrudes into the subarachnoid space.8 Fluid is thought to follow a pressure gradient through the defect into the retinal stroma and subretinal space. The source of the fluid may be liquified vitreous and/or cerebrospinal fluid.8,9A period of observation is recommended since the macular fluid may spontaneously resolve, but persistent macular fluid may lead to permanently decreased vision to the 20/200 level or worse. The optimal treatment is debated, but vitrectomy alone may be sufficient in some.10A visit 2 months later showed improved visual acuity to 20/20 and spontaneous regression of intraretinal and subretinal fluid. Latanoprost was stopped. Over the next 4 years, the patient remained stable without recurrent fluid or visual field changes.

question: A 49-year-old man with a history of diabetes, hypertension, intravenous drug abuse, and multiple sexual partners presented to the emergency department with painless vision loss in both eyes for 10 days, left eye worse than right eye, and photophobia in both eyes. His visual acuity was count fingers OD and 20/70 OS. Intraocular pressure was 20 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS. There were 1+ (10-12 cells/high-power field) anterior chamber cells in both eyes with very hazy posterior pole details in the right eye and minimal vitreous haze in the left eye. There was a hazy view to the posterior pole in the right eye with disc edema and multiple flame hemorrhages surrounding the nerve. Examination of the posterior pole in the left eye revealed partial obstruction of all vessels and a complete halo on the disc with numerous flame hemorrhages emanating from and surrounding the optic nerve, along with a few dot blot hemorrhages within the macula (Figure). His blood pressure was 173/137 mm Hg, but the rest of his vital signs were normal.Widefield color image of the left eye of a 49-year-old man with acute loss of vision. There is marked hemorrhagic disc edema with flame hemorrhages emanating from and surrounding the optic nerve. What Would You Do Next?
opa: Obtain HIV and syphilis serology results
opd: Obtain computed tomographic scan of the brain
answer: Obtain HIV and syphilis serology results
explanation: In this patient with hemorrhagic optic neuritis and evidence of panuveitis, infection must first be ruled out before initiating any systemic corticosteroids (choice A). A patient with a history of drug use and many sexual partners further supports ruling out an infection, particularly syphilis and HIV. Idiopathic demyelinating optic neuritis is a common cause of optic nerve edema with abnormal visual function in patients younger than 50 years, although it typically does not present with panuveitis.1 Therefore, beginning methylprednisolone would not be appropriate without proper systemic workup (choice B). Cytomegalovirus optic neuritis should be on the differential diagnosis for any patient with substantial risk factors for HIV/AIDS, although there were no signs suggestive of cytomegalovirus retinitis on examination and therefore treatment with foscarnet is not appropriate (choice C). Intracranial imaging may be warranted in the evaluation of papilledema, but magnetic resonance imaging of the brain would be more appropriate than computed tomography of the head, as it better detects optic neuritis and cerebrospinal fluid outflow obstructions (choice D).1 Additionally, his subsequent blood pressure measurements lowered and his initial reading was felt to be transient in the setting of an emergency visit, and thus, hypertension was not felt to be the causative etiology.Syphilis, tuberculosis, HIV, Lyme disease, and Bartonella are common culprits of infectious optic neuropathies, so a detailed history on sexual practices, drug use, travel history, and exposure to cats should be taken.1 Primary syphilis includes a painless chancre; secondary syphilis includes a macular papular rash involving the palms and soles, condylomata lata, and lymphadenopathy; and tertiary syphilis includes gummas, aortitis, and tabes dorsalis. Ocular syphilis can occur at any stage of the syphilitic infection, and its varying, wide range of clinical presentations makes it known as the “great masquerader.”2,3 Since Treponema pallidum cannot be cultured in vitro, the diagnosis of syphilis relies on treponemal and nontreponemal serologic testing. Nontreponemal testing is generally used as an initial screening test, monitoring therapeutic response to treatment, and includes the rapid plasma reagin and Veneral Disease Research Laboratory (VRDL) tests.4 However, they may be associated with false-positive results in patients with autoimmune diseases, tuberculosis, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, pregnancy, rickettsia infections, and other spirochetal infections.2 Treponemal testing consists of the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption and Treponema microhemagglutin assay; since they are highly sensitive and specific for syphilis, they are traditionally used as confirmatory tests after nontreponemal testing, although they cannot be used to assess treatment response.5,6 Alternatively, the reverse syphilis testing algorithm begins with a treponemal test followed by a confirmatory nontreponemal test. This algorithm has a higher sensitivity in diagnosing primary and secondary syphilis at 98.3% compared with 72.9% via the traditional pathway.7,8HIV testing should be pursued in cases of suspected syphilis because of the high incidence of coinfection (20%-70%).6 Syphilis and HIV are mandatory reportable diseases in all 50 states. On positive fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test results and signs of ocular syphilis (especially with retinal or optic nerve involvement), an infectious disease specialist should be consulted and lumbar puncture should be performed with cerebral spinal fluid VRDL testing with repeated lumbar puncture to monitor for successful treatment.5,9,10 The treatment of neurosyphilis is with intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days; in the case of a penicillin allergy, desensitization (recommended), ceftriaxone, doxycycline, or tetracycline are alternatives.3,4 The visual outcome after treatment is variable, with syphilis uveitis having the most improvement and optic neuritis having poor visual prognosis.3,5,9Fundus autofluorescence did not reveal a classic placoid lesion, but his rapid plasma reagin test and syphilis antibody test results were both positive. HIV testing was negative. This patient was treated with intravenous penicillin (after desensitization) and lumbar puncture, which returned a positive VDRL result. The patient returned 1 year later with improvement of visual acuity to 20/40 OU with resolution of his disc edema in both eyes.
