opb: Carcinomatous meningitis–primary adenocarcinoma of the lung
diagnosis: A. Primary central nervous system lymphoma–leptomeningeal variant
answer: Primary central nervous system lymphoma–leptomeningeal variant
explanation: Our patient presented with subacute, progressive cranial neuropathies and lumbosacral radiculopathies, with magnetic resonance imaging showing multifocal leptomeningeal enhancement and a CSF profile with lymphocytic pleocytosis and hypoglycorrhachia. Alternate diagnostic considerations included neurosarcoidosis, which was determined improbable given absence of lymphadenopathy without radiologic evidence of granulomas and negative serum angiotensin-converting enzyme study results. A primary carcinoma was determined unlikely given absence on repeated CSF cytology and negative positron emission tomography of the body. Tuberculosis was also considered and presumptively treated despite repeated negative CSF acid fast bacilli staining pending an ultimately negative serum quantiferon result.The patient’s neurologic condition progressively deteriorated and he died.  Autopsy performed 3 months after presentation revealed a non-Hodgkin diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with predominant involvement of the leptomeninges.  Pathological hematoxylin-eosin staining at autopsy revealed primary CNS lymphoma with characteristic angiocentric pattern of lymphocyte aggregation, further supported with positive B-cell and neoplasia markers (Figure 2).Cross-section of decedent's lumbar spine, showing multifocal infiltration of neural tissue by pockets of medium-to-large atypical lymphoid cells with open chromatin, increased cytoplasm, and variable mitotic activity on hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×10). Additional immunohistochemical staining revealed a predominance of CD20-positive cells, with a small amount of admixed CD-3 positive cells, and also detected CD 10, Bcl-6 and MUM1 a pattern consistent with a diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell Lymphoma.In 2013, the International Primary CNS Lymphoma Collaborative Group1 identified a subset of 48 patients with sole leptomeningeal disease without parenchymal involvement.  This study, to our knowledge, is the most comprehensive regarding evaluation of epidemiology, diagnosis, and treatment of this rare form of CNS lymphoma specifying the subset primary leptomeningeal lymphoma variant primary CNS lymphoma. According to this study, among immunocompetent individuals, primary leptomeningeal lymphoma has a slight male predominance, with median age at onset in the early 50s. Clinical presentation reveals a predilection for cranial neuropathies and lumbar radiculopathies. Magnetic resonance imaging findings reveal leptomeningeal enhancement without obvious parenchymal involvement. Pathologic findings with cytology are diagnostic in 67% of patients, and flow cytometry and gene rearrangement studies reveal monoclonal B- or T-cell populations in 80% of cases. Cerebrospinal fluid profiles are abnormal in all patients, showing leukocytosis (median white blood cell count, 96/× 103/μL; 90% lymphocytes), hyperproteinemia (median protein level, 235 g/dL), and hypoglycorrhachia (median glucose, 47 mg/dL). The lymphoma subtype is most frequently non-Hodgkin, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.1  In one-third of cases a meningeal biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. Treatment depends on the functional status of the patient at presentation, although typically involves chemotherapy with or without whole-brain radiation therapy.1The study by Taylor et al1 did not report autopsy findings in their cohort, as their patients were identified with CSF studies and meningeal biopsies.  Our case illustrates a rare variant of primary CNS lymphoma, which despite multiple CSF samples and meningeal biopsies, ultimately required autopsy for diagnostic confirmation.

question: A woman in her 60s presented with a 6-month history of itchy eruptions that initially started on the arms and then spread to involve the lower legs. The patient admitted to occasional burning sensation of new lesions. On review of systems, the patient denied fevers, fatigue, myalgias, arthritis, shortness of breath, oral ulcers, and recent infections. Clinical examination revealed several erythematous patches and plaques on the arms and lower legs, and nontender violaceous firm nodules on the elbows, wrist, ankle, interphalangeal, and metatarsophalangeal joints (Figure 1A and B). There was no lymphadenopathy present. A punch biopsy specimen from a plaque on the right forearm was obtained (Figure 1C and D). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: The biopsy specimen revealed a diffuse dermal, perivascular, and periadnexal neutrophilic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils and extravasated erythrocytes (Figure 1C). Karyorrhexis and areas of vasculopathic changes were also noted (Figure 1D). Papillary dermal edema was not seen. A periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain failed to highlight fungal organisms. Clinicohistopathologic correlation supported the diagnosis of erythema elevatum diutinum (EED).The patient was started on dapsone, 100 mg daily, which provided rapid improvement and subsequent resolution of all plaques and nodules within 2 months.Erythema elevatum diutinum (EED), first described by Hutchinson in the 1800s,1 is a rare chronic dermatosis that often presents as red-brown to purple plaques and nodules on the extensor surfaces of the extremities.2 The exact etiology remains unknown, but it is thought to be caused by vascular mediated immune complex deposition that activates the complement cascade and initiates a leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV).3,4The disease has not been found to have sex or race predilection, but commonly occurs in adults aged 30 to 60 years.5,6 However, it is important to note that EED may present earlier and more advanced in patients with HIV.6 Erythema elevatum diutinum  is associated with a variety of underlying systemic diseases including autoimmune (rheumatoid arthritis), infectious (streptococcal), and hematological, particularly IgA monoclonal gammopathy.7,8Most patients present in stable condition with occasional arthralgia and constitutional symptoms.6 A few cases have reported ocular involvement,3 prompting early ophthalmologic evaluation. Clinically EED presents as persistent, firm, erythematous to violaceous papules, plaques, and nodules with symmetrical distribution,7 particularly over the joints of the hands, feet, elbows, and knees. Rarely, lesions may bullous or ulcerate. Our patient had involvement of the elbows, hands, interphalangeal, and metatarsophalangeal joints. In a few cases lesions have occurred on the face, ears, and truncal region.4,8 Although lesions are often asymptomatic, patients have experienced pruritus, tenderness, and local burning sensation.2,4,8 Our patient shared similar symptoms with new-onset lesions.Erythmia elevatum diutinum has similarities to a variety of cutaneous diseases, making the potential for differential diagnoses vast. In early stages of the disease, this includes Sweet syndrome, pyoderma gangrenosum, granuloma annulare, and erythema multiforme.6,8 In the late stage, dermatofibroma, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, Kaposi sarcoma, and bacillary angiomatosis are also considered.4Histologically, early lesions of EED are characterized by an LCV with an infiltrate of neutrophils and fibrin deposition in the dermis.4,7 Early stages may often resemble Sweet syndrome but the presence of LCV distinguishes EED.6 During the progression of the disease, more histiocytes and spindle cell proliferation may be seen and histologically may resemble dermatofibromas, granuloma annulare, and fibrous histiocytoma.7 Late-stage histologic findings tend to show increased granulation tissue, dermal fibrosis, and blood vessel dilatation and proliferation, likely a consequence of continued dermal inflammation. The use of special stains and immunofixation electrophoresis may be necessary to rule out any infectious or monoclonal gammopathy etiologies.Treatment for EED is difficult because of its chronic and relapsing course. The disease is usually benign and tends to resolve after 5 to 10 years,1 with a few cases lasting up to 25 years in patients with underlying systemic disease.9 Dapsone is considered first-line treatment for early lesions.2,4 In patients for whom dapsone is not effective, colchicine, tetracycline, and systemic steroids have been used with limited success.4,5 In late-stage lesions, the use of intralesional corticosteroids and surgical excision has shown promising results.10 Patients with underlying disorders or infections should have targeted treatment at the underlying etiology, because this may improve EED outcomes.4Erythmia elevatum diutinum  is a chronic recurring skin disorder with numerous clinical imitators. It may be associated with several autoimmune, infectious, and hematological disorders. Therefore, it is important to make a correct diagnosis and identify associated disorders to provide optimal treatment.

question: A man in his 30s had ulceration of the skin of the soles, legs, hands, elbow joints, and face of 15 days’ duration. It had started as swelling of the feet, followed by erythematous acral lesions. Numbness of the hands and feet had begun 1½ years previously, spreading gradually to the forearm and legs. He had no history of fever, joint pains, or epistaxis. Black eschar and ulceration with purulent discharge was seen over the soles and elbows. There were triangular and bizarre purpuric and necrotic lesions over the legs, thighs, and dorsum of the hands (Figure, A) with necrosis of pinnae and nasolabial folds. The scrotum was also affected. There was diffuse infiltration of the face and madarosis of the lateral half of the eyebrows. He also had hypoesthesia over the palms, proximal forearms, feet, and legs. Peripheral nerve examination revealed thickening of the right radial cutaneous and both ulnar nerves. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was present. Findings from the rest of the general physical and systemic examination were normal. Punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, B-D).A, Multiple bizarrely shaped purpuric and necrotic plaques on the hands and lower limbs. Erosion is seen on the scrotum. B-D, Histopathologic images. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Biopsy showed necrotizing vasculitis of the small vessels in the upper dermis and endothelial proliferation of medium-sized vessel in the mid dermis (Figure, C). There was periappendageal and perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate containing foamy macrophages (Figure, B). The infiltrate extended up to the subcutaneous fat. Fite-Faraco stain revealed acid-fast bacilli in endothelial cells and a bacterial index (BI) of 6+ (Figure, D).Slit skin smear revealed a BI of 6+. Hemogram showed a hemoglobin level of 10 g/dL (100 g/L), total leukocyte count of 8200/μL(8.2×109/L), and a platelet count of 239 000/μL. Results from liver and kidney function tests; serum electrolytes, routine blood glucose, and urine tests; and microscopic evaluation were within normal limits. Electrocardiography and chest radiography results were normal. Results from human immunodeficiency virus serology and venereal disease research laboratory tests were negative.The patient was started on multibacillary multidrug therapy (MB MDT) regimen (rifampicin, 600 mg once a month; dapsone, 100 mg/d, clofazimine, 300 mg once a month and 50 mg/d) along with intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone, 1 g twice daily). Oral prednisolone was started with a dose of 40 mg/d and tapered over 3 weeks. The ulcers were cleaned and dressed with silver sulfadiazine. The patient’s condition improved over the next 3 weeks. He was discharged with the advice to continue MB MDT for 2 years under monthly follow-up.Lucio phenomenon is a type of reaction seen in diffuse form of lepromatous leprosy (LL) also called “pure and primitive diffuse lepromatosis.”1,2 The condition has been mainly described in Mexicans, with very rare reports from India.3-5Lucio leprosy is a nonnodular type of LL that presents as uniform, smooth, infiltrated skin, better felt than seen. The patients first notice numbness and impairment of sensation in the hands and feet; later, there is loss of eyebrows, eyelashes, and finally the body hair.2Lucio phenomenon appears as triangular or polygonal-shaped red patches, mainly on the extremities, that later become purpuric. The center of purpuric lesions becomes necrotic and ulcerated and finally develops a brown or black crust (eschar). On the legs, the ulceration may be larger with jagged edges surrounded by an inflammatory zone.1,2 There may be secondary pyoderma lesions and chronic cellulitis complicating the condition.2Clinically, Lucio phenomenon can resemble the necrotic variant of erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). However, there are certain differentiating features. Lucio leprosy is a diffuse infiltration of the skin in which the reaction occurs, whereas ENL occurs in LL with plaques and nodules. Lucio phenomenon is seen in untreated patients, but ENL is more frequent in patients receiving antileprosy treatment. Ulcers in Lucio phenomenon are small and superficial, while ENL ulcers are deep and may result in fibrotic scars. ENL lesions may be accompanied by systemic complaints, such as fever, arthralgia, myalgia, neuritis, iridocyclitis, orchitis, lymphadenopathy, nephritis, and hepatitis; however, these signs and symptoms are minimal or totally absent in Lucio’s phenomenon.6Lucio phenomenon can be differentiated histologically from ENL by features such as epidermal necrosis, necrotizing vasculitis of the superficial dermal vessels, severe focal endothelial proliferation of the mid-dermal vessels, and by the presence of large number of bacilli in endothelial cells.7Our patient had features of Lucio leprosy with numbness preceding the loss of eyebrows and skin infiltration. The symptoms of Lucio phenomenon developed 1½ years after the onset of numbness. The clinical picture was characteristic, with necrotic lesions located chiefly on the extremities. Also, there was absence of fever, joint pain, and other constitutional symptoms. The histological findings of vasculitis of the small upper dermal vessels, endothelial proliferation of the mid-dermal vessel, and presence of acid-fast bacilli within the endothelial cells confirmed the diagnosis.MB-MDT remains the mainstay of treatment. Although steroids have a good effect, thalidomide is of no value.1 Our patient improved with MB-MDT, antibiotics, oral prednisolone, and local wound care.

question: A man in his 70s presented for evaluation of a nonhealing lesion of his left cheek. Examination of the head and neck revealed the incidental finding of bilateral auricular rigidity and immobility. Both ears appeared normal and were nontender and asymptomatic (Figure, A). The patient recalled that his barber had noted an increase in difficulty trimming hair in the areas around his auricles owing to their inflexibility. The only other notable finding was increased rigidity of his nasal cartilage. The patient denied any decrease in auditory acuity, frostbite, or any previous trauma to his ears. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and secondary chronic renal insufficiency, cardiovascular disease, and gout. His long-term medications included lisinopril, glipizide, terazosin, insulin glargine, labetalol, allopurinol, hydrochlorothiazide, and erythropoietin. An incisional biopsy of his left auricle was performed. Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the biopsy specimen showed regions of ossification and calcification (Figure, B). A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the head was performed within 2 weeks of his original biopsy and showed extensive calcification in the area of the auricles (Figure, C). The patient’s laboratory workup showed an elevated creatinine level of 1.8 mg/dL (reference range, 0.6-1.2 mg/dL), which had been his baseline level for the past 2 years. He had a hemoglobin level of 11.1 g/dL (reference range, 14-18 g/dL), which was felt to be secondary to his chronic renal failure. His serum calcium level  had been normal with the exception of an elevated value noted of 10.4 mg/dL noted 1 year ago (reference range, 8.7-10.2 mg/dL). His phosphorus, alkaline phosphorus, electrolyte, and AM cortisol levels; parathyroid function; and thyroid function were within normal limits.A, Photograph of ear. B, Photomicrograph of biopsy sample. C, Head computed tomographic image. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Histopathologic examination of the incisional biopsy shows exclusively regions of ossification with focal calcification (Figure, B). The patient’s head CT shows impressive radiodensity of the bilateral pinnae owing to calcification (Figure, C).Cutaneous calcification or ossification occurs when the factors that regulate the transport and concentration of calcium are altered. Calcification is the result of deposition of amorphous, insoluble calcium salts, while ossification occurs when calcium and phosphorous are deposited in a proteinaceous matrix as hydroxyapatite crystals.1,2 Ossification may follow calcification, but in most disorders, 1 of these 2 models of calcium deposition predominates.2Ossification of the auricle is extremely uncommon, with about 20 cases reported, the first by Bochdalek in 1866.3 Petrified ear is a type of calcinosis cutis that can subsequently undergo ossification in the elastic cartilage of the ear. This results in usually malleable ears becoming inflexible like solid bone. Review of the literature did not reveal any other cases in which the patient had calcification of the auricles and nasal cartilage, making this case distinctly unusual.4Petrified ear has been attributed to dystrophic calcification, metastatic calcification, and ectopic ossification. Dystrophic calcification occurs when damage to the tissue incites calcification with normal serum calcium and phosphorous levels. Examples include dermatomyositis, CREST syndrome (calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia), and trauma. Metastatic calcification occurs via a disturbance in calcium metabolism in which the serum calcium and phosphorus levels become elevated. Examples of this include chronic renal failure, adrenal insufficiency, sarcoidosis, and hyperparathyroidism.4 Ectopic ossification is believed to occur through the transformation of mesenchymal cells into osteoprogenitor cells.1 There are 3 conditions theorized to be needed for this transformation: the presence of inducing agents, osteogenic precursor cells, and a permissive environment.5 Hypothermia is the most common cause of auricular ossification, with rapid cooling causing vascular occlusion and thrombosis. The resulting ischemia incites lamellar bone proliferation. Other causes associated with ossification include trauma, perichondritis, diabetes mellitus, and Addison disease.4Patients with petrified ear usually present asymptomatically but may complain of discomfort or pressure when lying down or sleeping on the affected side. They may also report hearing impairment on the affected side or otalgia due to narrowing of the ear canal. Physical examination reveals an inability to fold the affected auricles but with sparing of the lobules. Evaluation of a patient with petrified ear should focus on underlying metabolic and endocrine abnormalities. Laboratory testing should include a routine radiograph; complete white blood count; basic metabolic profile; thyroid function tests; and parathyroid hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, cortisol, serum calcium, and phosphorus levels.Plain film radiographs of the skull in patients with petrified ear will show areas of hyperdensity in the auricles. Computed tomographic imaging will show areas of radiolucent spaces with dense opacities representing the pattern of trabecular bone. Histopathologic analysis is required for differentiating between calcification and ossification.6,7 Petrified ear is usually asymptomatic, early intervention rarely occurs, and therefore treatment options are limited. Wedge resection is an option for severe discomfort or hearing loss and in extreme cases surgical removal of all the affected portion of the ear can be performed.8,9In summary, petrified ear is a rare clinical event with varied causation. Although our patient had several comorbidities, we would assert that his underlying renal failure and attendant subclinical disordered calcium/phosphate metabolism may well have been etiologic. Routine evaluation in similar such cases should include evaluation of other cartilaginous sites as well as a workup to exclude frank metabolic and correctable abnormalities. Further case reporting may help to elucidate the pathophysiologic characteristics of petrified ear and eventuate in better treatment options.

question: A 61-year-old man with history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism presented for evaluation of neck pain, stiffness, and occipital headaches lasting 4 years. Acetaminophen and meloxicam provided only partial relief. He also noted progressive thickening of skin in the nape of his neck. He denied any prior history of Raynaud phenomenon; heart, kidney, or liver disease; diabetic retinopathy; nephropathy; or neuropathy. He had quit smoking 24 years ago and reported currently drinking 3 glasses of wine per week. His medications included rosiglitazone, glimepiride, and levothyroxine.On examination, he weighed 131.5 kg (body mass index, 40.57); his heart rate was 82/min and blood pressure was 161/89 mm Hg. He had facial swelling and brawny periorbital edema (Figure 1A). He also had a large area of diffuse, slightly erythematous, nonpitting woody induration extending from the nape of his neck (Figure 1B), to the upper back, shoulders, and upper arms. This resulted in limitation of range of motion of his neck. Examination of his heart, lungs, abdomen, and lower extremities was unremarkable.A, Facial swelling and periorbital edema. B, Woody induration involving the nape of neck and upper back.Laboratory testing showed a fasting blood glucose level of 178 mg/dL (9.9 mmol/L). Complete blood cell count, levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone and albumin, and the remainder of his comprehensive metabolic panel were normal. Urinalysis showed trace protein without blood. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 34 mm/h, C-reactive protein level was 0.3 mg/dL (2.9 nmol/L), and hemoglobin A1C level was 7.5%. An antinuclear antibody panel was negative. A magnetic resonance imaging scan of the cervical spine showed degenerative changes at the C5-C6 level and a marked increase in skin thickness posteriorly.Obtain a skin biopsy from the upper back What Would You Do Next?

explanation: C. Obtain a skin biopsy from the upper backThe key to the correct diagnosis is the woody induration and its characteristic distribution in this patient with diabetes. Establishing the clinical suspicion of scleredema diabeticorum requires a skin biopsy, which is the preferred course of action in this case (option C). Although periorbital edema can be seen in diabetic nephrotic syndrome (option A), normal serum albumin level and only trace proteinuria makes it unlikely. The absence of dyspnea or leg edema also makes congestive heart failure (option B) less likely. Superior mediastinal syndrome (option D) in this former smoker may cause facial and neck swelling but would not cause such woody induration. Other fibrosing skin conditions (eosinophilic fasciitis, scleromyxedema, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, and systemic sclerosis) have a distinctive history and clinical presentation and are thus not considered here.Scleredema is a skin and connective tissue condition characterized by nonpitting woody induration of the skin typically involving the nape of neck, interscapular region and upper and mid-back, and sometimes the face, upper chest, and upper arms. Usually, the distal extremities are spared. Sometimes there is marked facial involvement leading to periorbital edema (Figure 1A).1Scleredema has been described in 4 different clinical scenarios: (1) after certain infections (scleredema of Buschke), (2) associated with a circulating paraprotein, (3) an idiopathic form, and (4) associated with diabetes mellitus, also referred to as scleredema diabeticorum. Histopathologically the different subtypes of scleredema are indistinguishable.2The etiology of scleredema diabeticorum is unknown. It has been suggested that advanced glycation end products play a role in its pathogenesis.3 Cultured dermal fibroblasts show increased collagen production and elevated type I procollagen messenger RNA levels.4The prevalence of scleredema diabeticorum ranges between 2.5% to 14% among persons with diabetes, but it may be underrecognized.1 There is no clear geographic or sex predilection. Diabetes is generally poorly controlled, often requiring insulin, and frequently complicated by diabetic retinopathy and neuropathy. In these patients, scleredema diabeticorum starts insidiously and progresses gradually, with a mean age of onset of 54 years and a mean duration of diabetes at diagnosis of 13 years.5Skin biopsy shows noticeable thickening of the reticular dermis, due to increased deposition of collagen, which also extends into the subcutis (Figure 2). The collagen fibers are swollen and separated from one another, interspersed with deposits of mucin. There is accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, particularly hyaluronan, with concurrent dermal sclerosis. Increased mucin deposition can be highlighted with special stains, eg, colloidal iron (Figure 2, inset). Dermal appendages are preserved. Inflammatory cells are sparse, but mast cells are increased.4 Elastic fibers are reduced and fragmented.4Biopsy of skin from the upper back. Swollen collagen fibers (yellow arrowheads) separated by widened spaces filled with mucin (black arrowhead). There is normal cellularity of the dermis and no increase in fibroblasts (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×4). Inset: colloidal iron stain highlights increased mucin deposition (black arrowhead) between the collagen bundles (yellow arrowhead) (original magnification ×20).Improvement of glycemic control can sometimes partially reverse the skin changes.6 The role of corticosteroids and methotrexate is controversial.1 UV light therapy, in several forms, can sometimes be beneficial, including UVA1, psoralen and UVA, and photopheresis.1 Radiation (electron beam) therapy has also demonstrated some success.1Immunofixation electrophoresis was negative for a monoclonal protein. The patient was encouraged to lose weight and see an endocrinologist to achieve more stringent glycemic control. Other potential treatment options discussed above were not initiated. At follow-up 4 years later, he was found to have lost about 16 kg. His diabetes was under control. His neck pain and stiffness had abated, and there was noticeable improvement in the skin induration involving the nape of his neck and upper back.

question: A man in his 70s with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and a 50-pack-year smoking history presented with a worsening unproductive cough. Chest radiography identified a right lung nodule, with complete workup revealing a T2aN0M0 right upper lobe non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) measuring 4.3 × 2.9 cm. A clinically significant cardiac history precluded the option of surgery. He was treated with a definitive accelerated hypofractionated course of radiotherapy to a total of dose 60 Gy in 8 fractions. Acute toxic effects were not observed, with the exception of minor fatigue that resolved 1 month after treatment. A surveillance computed tomographic (CT) scan obtained at 3 months demonstrated that the right upper lobe tumor had decreased by 1 cm in all dimensions, and at this time the patient denied any new symptoms, including pain. Approximately 5 months after treatment, he awakened with abrupt onset of severe right shoulder pain. The pain was sharp, constant, and localized to his right scapula and ultimately progressed to the point of radiating down the extensor surface of his arm ending at his elbow. He denied paresthesias, weakness, or any inciting events that could have led to its onset. His primary care physician obtained a CT scan, followed 2 days later by a magnetic resonance image (MRI) of his right shoulder (Figure 1).Right shoulder diagnostic imaging 5 months after treatment. CT indicates computed tomography; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Hypofractionated radiotherapy (ie, stereotactic body radiotherapy [SBRT]) is the preferred modality of treatment for inoperable NSCLC, offering excellent local control.1,2 Chest wall pain is a known adverse effect of hypofractionated radiotherapy, with tumor location adjacent to the chest wall being the strongest predictor of toxic effects.3 In hopes of decreasing chest wall toxic effects, radiation oncologists frequently decrease the prescription dose or further fractionate the treatment (ie, smaller doses per day but more fractions).The biologically effective dose (BED) is used in radiation oncology for isoeffective dose calculations, most commonly to compare the potency of different dose-fractionation schemes. Onishi et al4 demonstrated a local control rate of 92% for patients receiving SBRT with a BED greater than 100 Gy, compared with 74% with a BED less than 100 Gy. Instead of our usual prescription of 60 Gy in 5 fractions for peripheral lesions, we delivered 60 Gy in 8 daily fractions5 with a volumetric modulated arc technique with 10 MeV photons given that the lesion was abutting the chest wall. The BED for the delivered regimen was 105 Gy.The T2-weighted MRI 5 months after radiation demonstrates a bandlike pattern of edema and inflammatory changes along the right posterolateral chest wall, with the 3500-cGy isodose line coinciding closely with the regions of T2 change (Figure 2). No rib fracture was identified on CT of the chest obtained 2 days prior to the MRI. The areas of inflammation include the subscapularis and serratus anterior muscles. It is possible the edema compressed the upper and lower subscapular nerves as well as the radial nerve—all arising from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.Radiation myositis is infrequently reported as skeletal muscle is relatively radio-resistant. question: An asymptomatic 47-year-old woman underwent a radiographic screening to rule out tuberculosis prior to volunteering at her local hospital. The incidental finding of a mediastinal mass prompted a referral to her primary care physician, who elicited from the patient some complaints of mild but worsening orthopnea that was exacerbated when she would lie down. She denied any recent weight loss, muscle weakness, or diplopia. Her surgical history was significant for having undergone a cesarean section. She denied any radiation exposure. A computed tomographic scan of the chest was obtained (Figure, A), and the patient was referred to surgery for evaluation.A, Computed tomographic scan of the chest revealing a mediastinal mass. B, Intraoperative dissection following median sternotomy.A physical examination identified a midline trachea, no significant thyromegaly in the neck, no significant lymphadenopathy, and no additional significant findings. The patient was taken to the operating room for surgery to remove the mass (with gross findings as seen in Figure, B). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: The anterior mediastinum is the most common site of mediastinal masses, which are most commonly goiters, thymomas, teratomas, mediastinal metastases, or lymphomas, with clinical and radiologic features aiding in the diagnosis.1 Substernal goiter has been the focus of surgical luminaries from Kocher2 to Lahey3 since its first characterization in 1749.4 Its pathophysiology is surmised to stem from a deficiency in iodine that can lead to decreased thyronine levels and a compensatory elevation in thyrotropin, thus causing thyroid hypertrophy and the development of goiter.5 The classic presentation is that of a woman in her fifth decade with an anterior mediastinal mass arising from the lower pole of the thyroid gland, supplied by the inferior thyroid artery. The theory behind this pattern of growth is the presence of anatomical barriers around the gland, superiorly by the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, posteriorly by the prevertebral fascia, and anteriorly by the strap muscles, leaving only the inferior area without a barrier to growth. Furthermore, the negative intrathoracic pressure accompanying swallowing and aided by gravity is thought to slowly bring an enlarging goiter to its substernal resting place.5 The majority of goiters are benign and are most commonly of the nodular goiter subtype.5Most patients tend to be asymptomatic, with only the occasional complaint of dysphagia related to mass effect. Computed tomography of the neck and chest is helpful in discerning anatomic relationships between the mass and adjacent structures, and in aiding preoperative planning.6 The treatment of choice for substernal goiter is surgical excision.5 The technical considerations of surgery deviate only slightly from traditional thyroidectomy; careful dissection is essential in locating the recurrent laryngeal nerve. With planar dissection, the goiter is then “delivered” into the cervical region.7 Traditional predictors of substernal goiters that require sternotomy include invasive thyroid cancers, a previous thyroidectomy, superior vena cava syndrome, isolated primary mediastinal tumors, a posterior mediastinal location, extension below the aortic arch, a gland mass of greater than 260 g, or an intrathoracic independent blood supply.7,8 Finally, while rare, tracheomalacia must be considered; although compression of the trachea can weaken the cartilage initially, the trachea may become dependent on the mass as a buttress.9 Following mass excision, airway collapse and negative-pressure pulmonary edema are chief concerns. These are best avoided with prolonged intubation and, occasionally, by a tracheostomy.9 Repair by tracheopexy with various meshes has been described.9 Novel approaches involving video-assisted thoracoscopic resection of mediastinal goiters have gained acceptance and represent an innovative solution to spare selected patients’ from undergoing a sternotomy.10

question: A teenage girl presented with recurrent episodes of palpitations for 6 consecutive years. The resting 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with no preexcitation or repolarization abnormalities. There were incessant multiple runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia with right bundle branch block morphologic features. QRS complexes were negative in the rest of the precordial leads (V2-V6) and in leads I and avL, but positive in III, avR, and avF, suggesting a left (lateral) ventricular apical origin (Figure 1). The echocardiogram showed no structural abnormalities. The patient was prescribed sotalol but her symptoms did not improve. Invasive electrophysiological mapping of the left ventricle endocardium demonstrated that the ventricular tachycardia probably originated from the epicardial surface of left ventricular apex.Twelve-lead surface electrocardiogram during tachycardia. diagnosis: Incessant ventricular tachycardia of unknown cause

explanation: Before considering further treatment options, careful evaluation of a possible substrate is necessary. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is superior to echocardiography, which had normal results in this case, in detecting small tumors and myocardial fibrosis.Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was requested for possible identification of a cause for the ventricular tachycardia and demonstrated a well-defined intramyocardial mass at the apical lateral wall of the left ventricle, bulging into the epicardial region. The lesion elicited low signals during the T1 and T2 black-blood sequences. Ten minutes after injection of a gadolinium-based contrast agent, the cardiac magnetic resonance image showed intense central contrast uptake with a surrounding nulled rim of myocardium, suggestive of fibroma (Figure 2A). The patient was referred to surgery where excision of a rounded 2-cm mass was performed. The tumor did not have a well-defined capsule and had to be removed by sharp dissection, including a thin layer of myocardial tissue that appeared to be mingled with the periphery of the firm tumor (Figure 2B). Histopathologic examination showed infiltrative margins of myocytes, proliferation of spindle cells, abundant network of collagen, and entrapped myocytes, confirming the diagnosis of primary cardiac fibroma (Figure 2C and D). The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and had no recurrence of the arrhythmia after the surgery.Cardiac magnetic resonance image. A, Intramyocardial mass at the apical lateral wall of the left ventricle bulging into the epicardial region. Late enhancement with a gadolinium-based contrast agent showed intense central contrast uptake with a surrounding nulled rim of myocardium, suggestive of fibroma. B, Surgical excision of a nonencapsulated, rounded, 2-cm mass from the left ventricular apico-lateral wall. C, Low-power section of the tumor tissue showing myocytes infiltrating into abundant collagen bundles (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×2.5). D, High-power section of the margin of the tumor tissue showing infiltrative myocytes, proliferation of spindle cells, abundant network of collage, and entrapped myocytes (Masson trichrome stain, original magnification ×40).This case emphasizes the importance of raising the suspicion of cardiac tumor as a cause of incessant tachycardia in children and young adults with otherwise normal resting electrocardiogram results. Fibroma is the second most common primary cardiac tumor in the pediatric population, after rhabdomyoma.1 Multiple previous reports have associated fibromas with ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death in the young.1,2 Although transthoracic echocardiography is usually the first line of imaging of cardiac tumors, it may miss small tumors owing to its limited field of view and limited resolution for soft tissue.3 Transesophageal echocardiography provides better views but still has limited tissue characterization abilities. Therefore, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is considered the criterion standard for assessment of suspected cardiac tumors. Reentry is the widely acceptable mechanism of arrhythmia, as most fibromas present with monomorphic ventricular arrhythmias; however, triggered activity cannot be excluded.2 Ventricular tachycardia was successfully induced and entrained during electrophysiological testing in a few reported cases.2 In our patient, the histopathologic findings showed islands of myocardium embedded within the network of collagen and fibroblasts. This finding provides further evidence supporting reentry as the mechanism of tachycardia in cardiac fibromas. Surgical excision of the tumor was curative for the clinical arrhythmia. During a 3-month follow-up period, the patient remained symptom free and a second electrocardiogram showed no recurrence of the ventricular tachycardia.

She denied any history of serious infections, including tuberculosis and syphilis, and denied having family members with visual difficulties. Her ocular history was remarkable only for bilateral cataract surgery by phacoemulsification many years prior. question: A woman in her late 50s presented to the clinic with severe right eye pain and a headache for the past 2 days. Her ophthalmic history was significant for mixed-mechanism glaucoma due to uveitis and chronic angle closure with prior implantation of bilateral superotemporal Baerveldt drainage implants. Her intraocular pressure (IOP) was controlled with topical brinzolamide. In addition, she had Fuchs corneal dystrophy. A month earlier, she had undergone Baerveldt implant repositioning from the anterior chamber to the sulcus in the right eye in preparation for future Descemet stripping endothelial keratoplasty owing to severe corneal decompensation. At that time, visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 ft OD. She was discharged with therapy including topical steroids, antibiotics, and atropine sulfate. On the first postoperative visit, IOP was 14 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation. On postoperative day 11, IOP remained stable at 7 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation and topical atropine was discontinued. At presentation 3 weeks postoperatively, IOP was 30 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation. Her visual acuity worsened from counting fingers to hand motions. Slitlamp examination of the right eye revealed a superotemporal Baerveldt drainage implant with fluid over the plate. High-resolution ultrasonography was performed (Figure).High-resolution B-scan ultrasonographic image of the right eye. explanation: Glaucoma drainage implants (GDIs) are a mainstay of treatment for patients with glaucoma refractory to topical IOP-lowering agents.1 Several studies have demonstrated that aqueous shunts provide comparable benefits with trabeculectomy and may in fact be associated with fewer postoperative complications. In the Tube Versus Trabeculectomy Study, early postoperative complications were less frequent in the tube group compared with the trabeculectomy group, with postoperative complication rates of 21% and 37%, respectively.2Glaucoma drainage implants can be classified as either functionally valved or nonvalved. While valved tubes such as the Ahmed and Krupin GDIs have some form of flow restriction, nonvalved GDIs such as the Baerveldt and Molteno GDIs are open.3 Common postoperative complications of GDIs include a shallow or flat anterior chamber and/or hypotony, corneal edema or decompensation, choroidal effusion, hyphema, and tube obstruction.3Tube shunts may be obstructed with blood, fibrin, vitreous, or iris. In the Ahmed Baerveldt Comparison Study, the overall postoperative tube occlusion rate was 5%, and tube occlusion occurred more frequently in the Baerveldt GDI group compared with the Ahmed GDI group.4 Failure of a conjunctival bleb to form over the plate or an elevation of IOP warrants inspection of the tube for possible obstruction.3 To avoid obstruction, tubes placed in the anterior chamber are typically beveled anteriorly, whereas tubes placed in the sulcus are beveled posteriorly. In this case, the bevel was anterior as the initial tube placement was in the anterior chamber. In future cases, it would be advantageous to rebevel the tube in the event that it is moved from the anterior to posterior chamber if the length allows.Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate the patency of the tube. Management depends on the mechanism of obstruction. Occasionally, debris obstructing the tube opening can be removed with digital pressure over the plate. With blood or fibrin tube obstruction, injection of tissue plasminogen activator can dissolve the clot. If the tube is occluded by iris or inflammatory tissue, an argon or YAG laser can be used to remove the tissue. For tubes occluded with vitreous, vitrectomy is typically indicated as vitreous traction poses a risk of retinal detachment.3The patient underwent paracentesis and began treatment with atropine and systemic acetazolamide. Four months after transplantation, she continues to do well. Her visual acuity has improved to 20/60 −2 and her IOP remains stable at 6 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation. She continues to receive topical atropine.

Vitreous biopsy was positive for Mycobacterium chelonae. The organism may mimic the clinical presentation of Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis but grow slowly and stain poorly using traditional media and dyes.1 Prolonged low-grade intraocular inflammation, transient steroid responsiveness, and intracapsular precipitates suggest that M chelonae inhabits the capsular bag.1Mycobacterium chelonae is a gram-positive, acid-fast bacterium that can cause severe, recalcitrant, and both focal and disseminated infections associated with trauma, indwelling catheters, surgery, chronic illnesses, or immunosuppressive agents.2 Intravitreal antibiotics, without vitrectomy, cure most cases of postlensectomy endophthalmitis3; however, rare reports of M chelonae endophthalmitis have described severe vision loss.4Pars plana vitrectomy with capsule and intraocular lens removal as well as administration of intravitreal vancomycin were performed. Final sensitivities of M chelonae in our case showed resistance to both cephalosporins and vancomycin, which were administered both early and late in the clinical course. The aphakic eye remained quiet without recurrent inflammation after definitive removal of the intraocular lens and capsule. The BCVA returned to the baseline value, and placement of an anterior chamber intraocular lens was planned.

question: A 50-year-old woman presented with a 20-year history of slowly progressive red-to-brown pruritic hyperkeratotic papules and reticulated hyperpigmentation involving her face, neck, chest, back, and upper and lower extremities (Figure, A and B). She was previously diagnosed with Darier disease after biopsy revealed acantholytic dyskeratosis. She was treated with fluorouracil and tazarotene, 0.1%, cream with mild improvement, but she continued to develop new lesions. Social, family, and past medical history were noncontributory. Physical examination revealed reddish-brown hyperkeratotic papules on the neck, trunk, and extremities and diffuse brown macules, many in a reticulated pattern, on the face, neck, trunk, and extremities. There were no nail or mucosal changes. Laboratory data was noncontributory. A punch biopsy specimen was collected from both the arm and trunk and histologic examination was performed (Figure, C and D).Photographs of clinical findings of reticulate hyperpigmentation of the (A) neck and chest and (B) lower extremities. Hematoxylin-eosin of (C) hyperorthokeratosis, epidermal acanthosis and elongated epidermal rete ridges with bud-like filiform projections and suprapapillary plate thinning (original magnification ×4) and (D) focal acantholysis without dyskeratosis (original magnification ×10). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: The punch biopsy specimens from the arm and trunk both revealed hyperorthokeratosis of the stratum corneum with epidermal acanthosis and elongated epidermal rete ridges with budlike filiform projections and suprapapillary plate thinning (Figure C). There was hyperpigmentation of basal keratinocytes and focal acantholysis without dyskeratosis (Figure D). A perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered melanophages was seen within the superficial dermis.The patient was subsequently treated with acitretin, urea 40% cream, and triamcinolone 0.1% cream with mild improvement in her disease.Galli-Galli disease (GGD) is a rare yet benign genodermatosis characterized by slowly progressive and disfiguring reticulate hyperpigmentation of the flexures and reddish-brown hyperkeratotic scaly papules on the trunk and extremities that may be painful or pruritic. In addition, perioral scarring pitted scars and comedolike lesions can be rarely seen. Less than 15 cases of GGD have been reported in the literature. The age of onset is widely variable, ranging from early adolescence to late adult life.1 The existing literature suggests that males tend to be affected more than females.2Galli-Galli disease is clinically indistinguishable from Dowling-Degos disease (DDD) and shares characteristic histologic features of DDD but with the additional finding of suprabasal acantholysis. In fact, owing to their similarities, there has been dissent as to whether GGD is an acantholytic variant of DDD or an entity of its own. Galli-Galli disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion with variable penetrance. However, sporadic cases have also been reported and patients typically have a negative family history.3,4 Mutations identified in the keratin 5 gene on chromosome 12 have been implicated in the pathogenesis of GGD.5 This mutation causes premature termination of the keratin 5 polypeptide, affecting the intermediate filament cytoskeleton and disrupting the structural integrity of basal keratinocytes.1Histologic features of GGD shows characteristic downward protrusions of the rete ridges with concomitant focal acantholysis.4 Acantholysis is considered a sine qua non for the diagnosis of GGD.2,3 Dyskeratosis may be visualized on biopsy, but it is not necessary for diagnosis; however, the presence of dyskeratosis does not exclude the diagnosis of GGD. Direct and indirect immunofluorescence studies are typically normal.2 Laboratory results are characteristically within normal limits; however, peripheral eosinophilia may or may not be present.4,6Our patient was previously diagnosed with Darier disease, which can be differentiated from GGD by the lack of digitate proliferations of rete ridges on biopsy and more significant dyskeratosis.6 Furthermore, Darier disease manifests earlier clinically, is characterized by crusted yellow-brown papules rather than the lentigolike macules seen in GGD, and has nail and mucosal membrane involvement.2,6 Grover disease, another acantholytic dermatosis to be differentiated from GGD, is an acquired disorder typically affecting middle-aged or elderly men.6 It is characterized by intense pruritus and papulovesicular eruptions around the chest, back, and thighs. Involvement of the distal extremities and lentigolike macules are not common in Grover disease and instead suggest GGD.2,6 Histopathologically, Grover disease does not have lentiginous elongations of rete ridges.6 While GGD and DDD have a nearly identical clinical presentation, DDD more often manifests with pitted perioral acneiform scars and comedolike lesions.1 Nevertheless, GGD is chiefly distinguishable from DDD owing to the presence of acantholysis on biopsy in GGD.2,5,7 Lastly, unlike GGD, Kitamura disease presents with palmoplantar pits, breaks in the epidermal ridges on the palms and fingers, as well as acral hyperpigmentation, particularly on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet.1,6Treatment of GGD is generally unsatisfactory. question: A male neonate born prematurely at 27 weeks’ gestational age was noted to have a erythematous eruption at birth. The neonate was the product of a dichorionic, diamniotic twin pregnancy. The other twin did not have any dermatalogic abnormalities. They were born to a previously healthy woman who had been hospitalized 12 days prior for tocolytic therapy. One day prior to delivery, the mother was noted to have yeast on urinalysis. The presence of epithelial cells in the sample suggested vaginal contamination. Despite tocolytic therapy, labor ultimately progressed the following day and cesarean delivery was performed owing to breech presentation of the unaffected twin. Physical examination of the affected twin revealed an afebrile, 1200 g preterm infant. Skin examination showed 100 to 200 pink papules, 0.05 to 0.2 cm in size, distributed on the trunk, extensor upper arms, and upper legs (Figure, A and B). A subset of the lesions appeared vesiculopustular, but no fluid was evident after attempted unroofing. The diaper area, hands, feet, nails, and oral mucosa were unaffected. The second twin had normal cutaneous examination findings. Laboratory analysis revealed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 6000/μL, which was composed of 21% neutrophils, 38% lymphocytes, 24% monocytes, and 5% eosinophils. Gram stain of lesional scrapings did not reveal bacteria nor WBCs, though potassium hydroxide staining showed numerous yeast forms. Lesional polymerase chain reaction was negative for herpes simplex virus. Bacterial cultures from the skin and the blood were ultimately negative. The placentas from both neonates were sent for pathologic analysis (Figure, C and D).A, Pink papules and vesicopustules were noted on the trunk, arms, and extensor thighs, but spared the diaper area; B, morphology of lesions; C and D, histopathologic images of umbilical cord section. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Gross inspection of the placentas was unremarkable. Microscopic examination of the placenta from the affected twin showed acute subchorionitis, chorioamnionitis, and focal wedge-shaped inflammatory foci at the surface of the umbilical cord (Figure, C). Gomori methenamine silver staining highlighted fungal spores and hyphal elements. These findings are consistent with Candida infection (Figure, D). There was no evidence of fungal infection in the unaffected twin.The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B. There was no evidence of extracutaneous dissemination of Candida. The cutaneous eruption resolved within 72 hours.Congenital cutaneous candidiasis (CC) is acquired in utero from direct ascending spread of Candida from the maternal genital tract. The cutaneous lesions of CC are often present at birth and are most commonly distributed on the trunk and extensor extremities, but can be generalized. Sparing of the diaper area and mucosal surfaces is characteristic.1 Nail involvement is variably present.2 Lesions are 0.2- to 0.4-cm pink-red macules, papules, and vesiculopustules.3 Fulminant cases may show bullae, erosions, or even a diffuse burnlike dermatitis.4Congenital cutaneous candidiasis  is rare, with only about 100 cases reported in the literature.3 Risk factors for CC include maternal Candida vulvovaginitis (though most of these cases will not develop CC), the presence of a foreign body in the cervix and/or uterus, and prematurity.3 In this case, maternal Candida vulvovaginitis is suspected to have been present and likely served as a nidus for infection.In patients where CC is suspected, the diagnosis can be established by demonstrating spores and pseudohyphae in skin scrapings and/or by culture of organisms from cutaneous lesions.3  In the correct clinical setting, the diagnosis can also be confirmed by demonstrating the presence of fungal organisms within foci of inflammation in fetal adnexal structures.5  Funisits, inflammation of the umbilical cord, is a hallmark of CC, and can be appreciated microscopically as wedge-shaped inflammatory infiltrates in areas of invasion by Candida organisms.5  In this patient, the diagnosis was established by the presence of numerous yeast in skin scrapings and microscopic involvement of the umbilical cord by fungal organisms (Figure, C and D). Blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fungal cultures, as well as imaging studies, can be used to evaluate for disseminated disease. In this patient, results from such additional workup were negative for disease.Prompt initiation of treatment is critical and is an important factor in determining outcome.6 Prognosis is correlated with birthweight. Neonates weighing  less than 1000 g have a mortality rate of approximately 40%, compared with an 8% mortality rate in those weighing 1000 g or more.3 Treatment is most commonly amphotericin B. Congenital cutaneous candidiasis  is not generally thought to herald underlying immunodeficiency, and workup in this regard is not indicated.A curious observation in this case was that only 1 neonate was affected. Given that separate amniotic sacs and placentas were present in this diamniotic, dichorionic pregnancy, it is possible that direct infectious spread to only one fetus occurred. Along these lines, it has been observed that plaques of Candida in CC are typically found on the inferior pole of the amniotic sac and sometimes directly across from the internal cervical orifice,5 raising the possibility that if 1 fetus was positioned more closely to the internal cervical orifice, selective infection could occur. Indeed, in this case, ultrasonographic examination prior to birth showed that the affected twin was positioned more inferiorly, closest to the cervix, while the unaffected twin was positioned more superiorly in a transverse fashion (becoming breech just prior to cesarean delivery).To our knowledge, this report represents only the second published case of discordant CC in dichorionic, diamniotic twins.7

question: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-year history of gradually increasing blue discoloration of her ears. She had mild knee arthralgia that was treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). She was seeing an ophthalmologist annually regarding brown spots on both eyes diagnosed as conjunctival nevi. No other family members were similarly affected. As an infant, her mother had taken her to their physician owing to dark discoloration of her diapers, but this was not investigated further.Examination revealed slate blue macular pigmentation within the antihelix and conchal bowls of both ears (Figure, A). There were prominent dark brown deposits on the conjunctivae medial and lateral to the iris of both eyes (Figure, B). No other pigmentary changes were noted on the skin or mucosal surfaces. A punch biopsy specimen from the pigmented area on the left ear was obtained (Figure, C).A, Examination of the left ear revealing slate blue macular discoloration, most prominent over the antihelix. B, Examination of the left eye showing dark brown pigment deposition of the conjunctiva lateral to the iris. Similar deposits were seen medial to the iris, bilaterally in both eyes. C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain on punch biopsy specimen of pigmented area on left ear demonstrating large pigment deposit in the dermis and adjacent to the cartilage (original magnification ×150). What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: Histopathologic examination showed large deposits in the dermis, interspersed between collagen bundles adjacent to the cartilage (Figure, C). Urinary biochemical analysis was conducted revealing high levels of homogentisic acid, diagnostic for alkaptonuria.Our patient was referred to the Department of Inherited Metabolic Diseases at Guys and St Thomas’ Hospital, London, England, where she underwent further assessment, including a cardiac echocardiogram and bone scan that revealed osteoporosis. A computed tomographic scan of the knees confirmed degenerative changes.As treatment, our patient has been recommended to continue NSAIDs for her knee arthralgia. Oral bisphosphonates were commenced for osteoporosis. Nitisinone is being considered as a treatment for our patient.Alkaptonuria is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder. It is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase gene (HGD) on chromosome 3q13 (OMIM: 203500).1 Mutations in HGD prevent the production of homogentisic acid dehydrogenase, which is responsible for the breakdown of homogentisic acid (HA), an intermediate product in the tyrosine degradation pathway. The consequent rise in levels of HA results in polymerization and deposition of a melanin-like pigment within cartilaginous tissues, skin, bone, and mucosal surfaces. Homogentisic acid can also be excreted in urine and sweat. Other more common causes of ochronosis include exogenous ochronosis exposure to substances like phenol, mercury, hydroquinone, and antimalarials that lead to pigment deposition on the skin.The worldwide prevalence of alkaptonuria is 1 in a million births. The highest prevalence is in Slovakia with an estimated 1 in 19 000 people affected.2 Despite its presence from birth, patients usually present in adulthood, predominantly with joint symptoms due to pigment deposition within the hyaline articular cartilage of joints, known as ochronotic osteoarthropathy. This is 1 of the 3 distinct features of alkaptonuria, the other 2 being homogentisic aciduria and ochronosis. Each feature presents at a different stage in life. Homogentisic aciduria is present at birth and can lead to early diagnosis in children if darkening of the urine is noticed. Ochronosis, which develops secondary to polymerization of HA, occurs between the third and fifth decade of life with melanin-like pigment deposits within the ears and eyes.1 Other organs that may be affected include the heart valves, leading to aortic valve stenosis, and kidneys, where renal calculi and kidney failure can develop. Ochronotic osteoarthropathy begins around the fourth decade and predominantly affects the large weight-bearing joints, such as the knees, causing changes resembling osteoarthritis radiographically.3 The vertebrae are often affected, with osteophyte formation and stiffening of the intervertebral joints. Osteoporosis also occurs, and this is thought to be due to the effects of HA polymers on bone matrix and cross-linking of bone collagen.4Although life expectancy in patients with alkaptonuria is normal, the osteoarthropathy leads to significant morbidity. Therefore, the mainstay of treatment is joint symptom control with analgesia. Treatments aimed at reducing the levels of circulating HA include low-protein diets and vitamin C. Low protein diets have been used in children, but compliance is difficult. Also, their value in adult patients is equivocal. Some benefit has been demonstrated with high-dose vitamin C (1 g per day), owing to its antioxidant properties.5Nitisinone is currently the most promising treatment for patients with alkaptonuria. It is an oral herbicide that was originally discovered as an extract of the bottlebrush plant. It acts by inhibiting the formation of HA, thereby reducing circulating levels of HA and urinary HA excretion. In rodents, it has been shown to decrease pigment deposition within joints.6 The long-term benefits for symptom control and joint disease progression in humans treated is unknown. It is currently only licensed for the treatment of tyrosinaemia, but there are 3 ongoing international trials for its use in alkaptonuria with promising biochemical results.7

explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is awareness of cholesterol embolization as a complication of procedures requiring aortic instrumentation or manipulation. Recent disturbance of aortic artery plaques during the recent procedures likely precipitated cholesterol embolization in this patient. The history, along with the cutaneous findings and peripheral eosinophilia, is highly characteristic of the disease and is an indication to check for other damaged organs, including the kidneys, pancreas, retina, and gastrointestinal tract.More imaging studies are not indicated, given the history of a recent procedure involving aortic cannulation, but if no inciting cause can be identified, additional imaging may be necessary. Initiation of anticoagulation may worsen embolization by further destabilizing atheromatous plaques,1,2 although a causal link between anticoagulant and thrombolytic therapy and cholesterol embolization is debated; continuation of clinically indicated anticoagulation is recommended.1,2 Amputation may ultimately be indicated for necrotic digits but would not be the next appropriate action.Cholesterol embolization is a small- to medium-vessel disease caused by arterial embolization of debris from disrupted atherosclerotic plaques. It is usually seen in patients undergoing arterial catheterization, prolonged anticoagulation, or acute thrombolytic therapy, although spontaneous embolization can occur.3 The typical patient is an elderly man (more than 50% of patients present when older than 70 years) with cardiovascular disease.4 Skin is the most commonly involved organ in clinically apparent cases, with a frequency ranging from 35% to 96%.5 Presentation is usually subacute, with time from an inciting event to presentation ranging from days to months.3The presentation of cholesterol embolization may be nonspecific or complex and may involve multiple organ systems. Embolism in the descending aorta can cause ischemia in cutaneous and muscle tissue of the trunk and lower limb, kidneys, and gastrointestinal system. Confusion, vision change, and skin changes in the upper limbs may be seen if embolization occurs in or proximal to the ascending aortic arch. Livedo reticularis is the most frequent cutaneous change, although cyanosis, gangrene, ulceration, nodules, purpura, and petechiae may also be seen.5,6 Although purpuric toe lesions are a cutaneous manifestation of cholesterol embolization, this is nonspecific and can be seen with vasculitis or other vasculopathies. Constitutional manifestations of cholesterol embolism are common but nonspecific and include fever, anorexia, weight loss, fatigue, and myalgias.1 Patients may also present with acute elevations in blood pressure due to occlusion of vasculature by cholesterol crystals and renin release secondary to kidney ischemia.2,3 Laboratory abnormalities include eosinophilia, anemia, hypocomplementemia, and elevated erythocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level.1,5 Urinalysis and microscopy can help diagnose kidney involvement and may reveal proteinuria, pyuria, eosinophiluria, and hematuria.2,5A proposed clinical triad for diagnosis1 includes history of a precipitating factor,2 acute renal failure, and cutaneous or retinal manifestations.3,7 Biopsy is needed to definitively confirm the diagnosis. Peripheral biopsy from skin or muscle is recommended to avoid more invasive sites. Forgoing biopsy may be prudent when retinal cholesterol crystals, or Hollenhorst plaques, are seen, as they are strong evidence of the disease.2 For our patient, funduscopy was nondiagnostic.No therapeutic standard exists, but current literature recommends supportive treatment and aggressive control of risk factors, eg, statin therapy, antiplatelet therapy, and avoidance of further vascular instrumentation.3 Recent articles have reported 1-year survival rates of 69% to 87%, with approximately 1 in 3 patients developing clinically significant kidney injury.3-5 The most common cause of death after cholesterol embolization is cardiovascular, possibly attributable to high incidence of preexisting cardiovascular disease.3,8-10The patient’s kidney function continued to decline, with creatinine level peaking at 9.9 mg/dL despite dialysis. Liver function test results and levels of amylase and lipase were within normal limits. Biopsy of a purpuric skin lesion on the right foot showed medium-sized vasculature containing a thrombus with associated cholesterol clefting (Figure 2), confirming the diagnosis. Dialysis was eventually discontinued, and the patient was transitioned to hospice. The patient died shortly thereafter from renal failure less than 5 months after onset of symptoms.Biopsy of purpuric foot lesion. question: A 10-year-old girl developed an annular skin lesion on her anterior neck. The lesion, initially attributed to a bug bite by her mother, enlarged and developed central clearing. The patient lived in North Carolina with no recent travel or known tick bite. She had no symptoms other than mild local itching. After several weeks, the patient’s mother applied over-the-counter topical antifungal cream and the lesion faded. After 10 days of antifungal therapy, the patient was evaluated by her pediatrician. Examination results were normal except for a 2.0-cm annular lesion with central clearing and peripheral flaking (Figure). The pediatrician ordered serologic testing for Lyme disease, prescribed 14 days of doxycycline based on the results (Table), and referred the patient to an infectious disease specialist for evaluation.Complete 14 days of antibiotic treatment for Lyme disease. No further testing is indicated.Complete 14 days of antibiotic treatment for Lyme disease. Repeat Lyme disease serology in 1 month to evaluate response. What Would You Do Next

explanation: This patient had a negative 2-tiered serologic test result for Lyme disease. The first-tier enzyme immunoassay (EIA) was equivocal but second-tier immunoblots were negative. For testing to be positive, both tiers must be positive (ie, the EIA must be positive or equivocal followed by positive IgM or IgG bands). Since the patient’s lesion was inconsistent with Lyme disease and there was an alternate etiology (tinea corporis) that responded to antifungal treatment, no further testing or treatment for Lyme disease was indicated.Approximately 3.4 million Lyme disease tests are performed annually in the United States (cost, ≈$500 million).1 The standard of care for Lyme disease testing is 2-tiered serology. The first-tier EIA quantifies potential antibodies against Borrelia burgdorferi. If the EIA is positive or equivocal, second-tier immunoblotting is performed to detect antibodies against more specific B burgdorferi surface proteins. The Medicare midpoint reimbursement is $31.32 for first-tier EIA and $28.49 for second-tier immunoblots.2Sensitivity during early localized infection is low (<40%), while host immune response is developing but increases to 70% to 100% for patients with disseminated infection. Specificity is 98% to 100%.3,4 If 2-tiered serology is negative in patients with possible early infection, repeat serology 3 to 4 weeks later may demonstrate seroconversion. Because IgM and IgG antibodies can persist for years, serology is not useful to monitor response to treatment.Erythema migrans (EM), the characteristic skin lesion of early Lyme disease, is an expanding circular patch that usually reaches at least 5 cm in diameter (eFigure in the Supplement). Classically EM has a target-like appearance, but it can be confluent. This patient’s rash was not consistent with EM since it was present for more than 6 weeks and never exceeded 5 cm. Moreover, EM initially appears at the tick bite site. It is unlikely a parent or child would have missed an engorged tick on the anterior neck for more than 1 day. Residence in a low-incidence state with a rash inconsistent with EM suggests low pretest probability.5 Testing in this setting is not useful and risks a false-positive result.6Individually positive bands in the immunoblot are not clinically significant (eg, the 41-kDa antibody band in this patient exists in ≈ one-half of serum samples from healthy blood donors due to cross reaction with flagellar proteins from bacteria such as Escherichia coli and oral commensal flora).7 Misinterpretation can cause diagnostic errors and unnecessary antibiotic exposure.8Patients with EM who live in or have traveled to areas endemic for Lyme disease can be diagnosed clinically without testing. For all other patients—those with atypical early disease or signs of disseminated infection—laboratory testing is necessary. Testing patients with low epidemiologic risk is generally not useful, but if pursued, clinicians must recognize the high likelihood of false positives. Using EIA or immunoblot alone is insufficient for diagnosing Lyme disease because of reduced specificity and potential for false positives.3Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay of blood has low sensitivity because of the short duration of spirochetemia. PCR of synovial fluid or skin biopsy samples may be useful in certain clinical situations if specimens are available.3Laboratory-developed tests for Lyme disease are offered by some commercial laboratories claiming to specialize in Lyme disease testing. These nonstandardized tests lack adequate clinical validation and FDA clearance and are not recommended.10The patient was evaluated by an infectious disease consultant 1 week after beginning doxycycline. Based on a clinical diagnosis of tinea corporis and very low likelihood of Lyme disease, discontinuance of doxycycline and resumption of topical antifungal therapy were recommended. Four weeks later, the lesion faded and the child was well.Testing is generally not recommended for patients unlikely to have Lyme disease (inconsistent illness or lack of plausible exposure). In this setting, false-positive results are more likely than true positives.A lesion consistent with erythema migrans in a region known to be endemic for Lyme disease does not require diagnostic testing.The recommended 2-tiered serology for Lyme disease begins with an EIA. If the EIA is positive or equivocal, immunoblotting should be performed. Both a positive or equivocal EIA and sufficient number of immunoblot bands (≥2 of 3 IgM or ≥5 of 10 IgG) are required for a positive test.Clinicians interpreting test results should not focus on individual positive bands as these have no diagnostic value on their own.Patients with Lyme disease symptoms (>30 d) require positive IgG immunoblot results to confirm diagnosis.Nonstandard tests for Lyme disease and alternative immunoblot interpretations offered by some specialty laboratories lack clinical validation and are not recommended.

question: A man in his 70s with hypertension, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) presented for a second opinion regarding treatment of MDS. Three years prior he had developed neutropenia and mild thrombocytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy sample demonstrated refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia. Cytogenetic testing results were normal, and there were 5% bone marrow blasts. The patient was treated initially with cyanocobalamin 250 micrograms daily, then danazol 200 milligrams 3 times daily, then epoietin α 60,000 units weekly. Filgrastim 300 micrograms weekly was added to epoietin α to attempt to augment response after 1 year of therapy. After approximately 2 years, he developed more pronounced cytopenias and presented with a white blood cell count of 2100/μL(480 neutrophils), hemoglobin level of 8.4 g/dL, and platelet count of 92 000/μL. He noted fatigue, but otherwise felt well. Physical examination revealed an isolated, symptomatic polypoid mass involving his right upper labial mucosa (Figure). It had been recently biopsied without definitive diagnosis, but since the biopsy, the mass had increased in size.An isolated polypoid mass affecting the right upper labial mucosa. What Is Your Diagnosis?
explanation: A bone marrow biopsy was repeated and demonstrated persistent MDS with 10% blasts and an abnormal karyotype: 46,XY,del(16)(q11.1). The patient was referred to the oral medicine unit for further evaluation and treatment of the isolated lip lesion. A fine-needle aspiration was performed, which revealed atypical mononuclear cells suspicious for blasts, and flow cytometry demonstrated the following immunophenotype consistent with myeloid sarcoma: CD45(dim)+ CD11B+ CD13+ CD33(var)+ CD34− CD64(predominantly)−CD117(var)+ HLA-DR(predominantly)−.Myeloid sarcoma is a rare extramedullary tumor of immature myeloid cells, or acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in the solid tumor phase. It occurs in less than 10% of patients with AML and only rarely antedates systemic bone marrow AML.1 In MDS, the incidence of myeloid sarcoma is less well characterized, but in the 30-year period from January 1965 to January 1994, only 46 cases of extramedullary myeloid tumor (including leukemia cutis) were reported.2 Interestingly, AML with bone marrow involvement developed in only 47% of these patients at a mean of 38 weeks from the initial extramedullary myeloid tumor.2 The much lower incidence of progression to AML with bone marrow involvement in MDS-associated myeloid sarcoma stands in contrast to truly isolated myeloid sarcoma, in which progression to AML with bone marrow involvement invariably occurs. Perhaps owing to the much lower incidence of progression to overt AML in MDS-associated myeloid sarcoma, patients who received chemotherapy for MDS-associated myeloid sarcoma demonstrated inferior survival compared with those who received conservative therapy only.2In addition to myeloid sarcoma and leukemia cutis, MDS can have protean autoimmune manifestations that have an effect on multiple organ systems. Of patients with MDS, 10% to 30% show signs of autoimmune disease, including vasculitis, seronegative polyarthritis, and skin lesions, including Sweet syndrome and pyoderma gangrenosum.3 Treatment for autoimmune manifestations of MDS includes corticosteroids and treatment for the underlying disease, the mainstay of which in high-risk disease is hypomethylating agents.Myeloid sarcoma most frequently occurs in the soft tissues, bones, periosteum and lymph nodes.1 Intraoral myeloid sarcoma lesions are rare and commonly present as a symptomatic enlargement of the gingiva, palate and/or buccal mucosa.4,5 Intraoral lesions are considered clinically aggressive with possible invasion of adjacent soft and/or hard tissues.4 These tumors often have a nonspecific clinical and histological appearance; however, immunohistochemical analysis can establish a definitive diagnosis.6,7Isolated myeloid sarcoma invariably is followed by systemic involvement with acute myeloid leukemia and, therefore, if the patient is an appropriate candidate for intensive induction chemotherapy, he or she should be treated with such, similar to systemic AML. In addition, radiation therapy can have a role in the treatment of myeloid sarcoma. It can be used as a consolidative strategy following induction chemotherapy for isolated myeloid sarcoma, for rapid debulking and symptom control, or for palliation in patients who are not appropriate candidates for intensive induction chemotherapy.1In the case described herein, age and comorbid conditions precluded treatment with intensive induction chemotherapy, and the myeloid sarcoma was treated with radiation therapy. The patient received 30 Gy in 15 fractions via 9 MeV electron therapy with complete response. It is known that radiation therapy can achieve durable disease control at the targeted site,8 though the therapy is not definitive if there is bone marrow involvement with malignant abnormalities.With regard to his bone marrow disease, the patient began therapy with 5-azacitadine, 75 mg/m2 on days 1 to 5 and 8 to 9 each month. After 3 cycles, his hemoglobin level and platelet counts normalized and his absolute neutrophil count was approximately 800/μL. He has not been hospitalized and enjoys a good quality of life with mild fatigue continuing to be his major symptom. Interestingly, his del(16)(q11.1) cytogenetic abnormality had been previously described as being associated with myeloid sarcoma.9 This case highlights development of myeloid sarcoma in patients who do not have frank involvement with AML in the bone marrow. Suspicion of myeloid sarcoma was heightened because the patient demonstrated clinical signs of MDS progression.
